```go
pgq := fts.Raw("fox:* & !hen").Config("english") // to_tsquery text
litq := fts.Raw(`fox NOT hen`)                    // FTS5 query
myq := fts.Raw("+fox -hen")                       // boolean-mode text
```

On MySQL and MariaDB `fts.Search` and `fts.Score` always use boolean mode with
a string built from the parsed words, so no typed character acts as an
operator. For natural-language mode or query expansion, which have no portable
form, use `fts.MySQLMatch` and `fts.MySQLRelevance` with a mode of your own.
The text is passed as given, so in `fts.Boolean` mode you own its operators.

<!-- docscheck:fragment -->

```go
cols := []momo.Column[string]{articleTitle, articleBody}
rel := fts.MySQLRelevance(cols, userInput, fts.NaturalLanguage)

hits, err := momo.Select[Hit](db).
	From(momo.TableRef{Name: "articles"}).
	Columns(articleID, rel.As("relevance")).
	Where(fts.MySQLMatch(cols, userInput, fts.NaturalLanguage)).
	OrderBy(rel.Desc()).
	All(ctx)
```

The columns must be exactly the columns of one `FULLTEXT` index, in its order.
A `MATCH` without such an index is `ErrValidation`, not the server's error 1191.
Both builders fail the build with `ErrUnsupported` on PostgreSQL and SQLite.

## How the dialects differ

| Feature                | PostgreSQL                                               | SQLite                                         | MySQL and MariaDB                        |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Index type             | GIN on a stored generated tsvector column                | external-content FTS5 table and sync triggers  | InnoDB `FULLTEXT` index                  |
| Query syntax           | `@@` with a tsquery                                      | FTS5 `MATCH`                                   | `MATCH ... AGAINST (? IN BOOLEAN MODE)`  |
| Ranking direction      | `ts_rank_cd`, higher is better                           | `bm25` is lower-is-better, `fts.Score` negates | the `MATCH` value, higher is better      |
| Stop words             | by configuration (`english` has them, `simple` has none) | none with the `unicode61` tokenizer            | the InnoDB list, set by server variables |
| Minimum token length   | none                                                     | none                                           | `innodb_ft_min_token_size`, 3 by default |
| Phrase                 | the `<->` operator                                       | a quoted string, exact adjacency               | a quoted string in boolean mode          |
| Prefix                 | `:*` in tsquery text                                     | `"pre"*`                                       | a trailing `*`                           |
| Snippet                | `ts_headline`                                            | `snippet()`                                    | `ErrUnsupported`                         |
| Transaction visibility | a write is visible in its own transaction                | a write is visible in its own transaction      | only committed rows                      |

## Limits

- Stop words. PostgreSQL drops the stop words of the configuration, so a phrase
  such as "the cat" can reduce to one word. MySQL InnoDB drops the words of its
  default stop word list unless `innodb_ft_enable_stopword` is off or a user
  list is set. A required term that is a stop word matches nothing, so a
  search that needs `the` or `it` finds nothing. SQLite `unicode61` has no
  stop words.
- Minimum token length. InnoDB does not index a word shorter than
  `innodb_ft_min_token_size` (3 by default), so a search for a two-letter word
  finds nothing, even in rows that contain it. A prefix shorter than that still
  matches the longer indexed words that start with it. The server settings are
  applied when the index is built, so changing one needs an index rebuild.
- Committed rows only. On MySQL and MariaDB a row inserted or updated in an open
  transaction is not found by a search, in the same transaction or any other,
  until the transaction commits. Inserting and then searching inside one
  `db.Tx` returns nothing. PostgreSQL and SQLite index changes are
  transactional: the search sees them inside the transaction, and a rollback
  removes them.
- MySQL boolean mode has no prefix phrase. A required prefix phrase such as
  `well-kn*` is rendered as `+well +kn*`, so it also matches rows that hold
  the words apart. An excluded prefix phrase is rendered as the exact phrase
  without the wildcard (`-"well kn"`), so it never excludes more than the
  phrase.
- A PostgreSQL tsvector is limited to 1 MB per value. A longer value is a
  database error, not a silent cut.
- A MySQL `FULLTEXT` index covers at most 16 columns.
- Collation and case. FTS5 `unicode61` folds case and removes diacritics by
  default. A PostgreSQL configuration lowercases but keeps diacritics unless
  `unaccent` is added to it. MySQL follows the column collation. The same text
  can therefore match differently on each dialect.
- NULL. A NULL column contributes nothing, and a row whose searchable columns
  are all NULL never matches.
- A search that cannot run fails with a momo error, not the driver's text: a
  missing FTS5 build or table is `ErrUnsupported`, a missing `FULLTEXT` index
  or a configuration that differs from the index is `ErrValidation`.

## Inspection and migration tools

`momo migrate diff` compares the declaration, with the structures each dialect
derives from it, against the snapshot and writes the SQL above. A second `diff`
after `apply` is empty. `momo migrate validate` and `AutoMigrate` apply the same
checks. `momo migrate drift` and `generate --from-db` read the database back:

- PostgreSQL: a stored generated column and its GIN index, written in the shape
  momo renders, read back as the declaration with its configuration, columns and
  weights; so is a GIN index on a `to_tsvector` expression of that shape. Any
  other tsvector column or expression stays a plain index.
- SQLite: an external-content FTS5 table is read from `sqlite_master` with its
  columns and tokenizer. The shadow tables of an FTS5 table stay hidden, and a
  virtual table of another module, or an FTS5 table with an option the
  declaration has no field for, is not reported as a declaration. The sync
  triggers are ordinary triggers: `momo migrate drift` reports a missing or
  altered one.
- MySQL and MariaDB: an index of type `FULLTEXT` is read as the declaration, and
  on MySQL its parser comes from `SHOW CREATE TABLE`. The storage engine of a
  table that is not InnoDB is read too, which `AutoMigrate` uses to refuse a
  declaration on it.

`generate --from-db` writes the `search` tag when it says everything (a
declaration on SQLite, MySQL or MariaDB named `<table>_search`, with no option)
and `c.FullText` otherwise. It writes no field for the generated tsvector
column of PostgreSQL and none for the sync triggers of SQLite, because the
declaration implies them. A full-text index the models cannot declare is
reported as a warning and left out.

## Hybrid search

`momo.HybridSearch` fuses a full-text leg and a cosine-distance vector leg with
reciprocal rank fusion. It runs on PostgreSQL, on SQLite (FTS5 and sqlite-vec,
so the cgo driver) and on MariaDB 11.8. MySQL has no vector distance function,
so on MySQL the call fails with `ErrUnsupported` before any SQL is sent; it
never falls back to a text-only search.

On SQLite and MariaDB the text leg searches the structure of the model's
declaration, the FTS5 table ordered by `bm25` or a boolean-mode `MATCH` over
all declared columns. `HybridSpec.Text` must be one of the declared columns, or
the call is `ErrValidation`. `HybridSpec.TextConfig` is ignored there, and
`HybridSpec.Query` is read like a `fts.Web` query. A query without a positive
word leaves the text leg empty and the result is the vector leg alone. On
MariaDB the text leg inherits the stop word, minimum token length and
committed-rows limits above, so a row inserted in the same transaction appears
through the vector leg only. See [hybrid search](vectors.md#hybrid-search) for
the knobs, the tie-breaks and the PostgreSQL leg.

## The column

PostgreSQL full-text search keeps a column type and the typed builders it had
before the portable calls. Every builder in this part returns `ErrUnsupported`
when the statement is built for SQLite or MySQL; use the calls above on those
dialects.

A model field of type `types.TSVector` maps to a `tsvector` column (and a
`types.TSQuery` field to `tsquery`). Both are codecs, so the generator and
`migrate` pick the column type from the Go type, diff it and read it back from
the database with no drift. The Go value is the text form PostgreSQL prints,
for example `'cat':3 'fat':2`. A nullable column is a `*types.TSVector`.

A declaration with `c.FullText` needs no such field: momo derives a generated
column. To maintain the column yourself, leave it nil on insert and update (the
application normally never sets it: the trigger overwrites it). Keep it current
with a trigger declared in `MomoConfig`, and index it with GIN:

<!-- docscheck:fragment -->

```go
type Article struct {
	momo.Model `momo:"table:kb_articles"`
	ID         int64            `momo:"pk,identity"`
	Title      string
	Body       string
	SearchTsv  *types.TSVector
	Embedding  vector.Vector `momo:"dim:1536"`
}

func (a *Article) MomoConfig(c *momo.Config) {
	c.Index("kb_articles_search_gin", &a.SearchTsv).Method("gin")
	c.Function(schema.Function{
		Name: "kb_articles_tsv", Returns: "trigger", Language: "plpgsql", Volatility: "VOLATILE",
		Body: "BEGIN NEW.search_tsv := setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(NEW.title, '')), 'A') || " +
			"to_tsvector('english', coalesce(NEW.body, '')); RETURN NEW; END;",
	})
	c.Trigger(schema.Trigger{
		Table: "kb_articles", Name: "kb_articles_tsv_trg", Timing: "BEFORE",
		Events: []string{"INSERT", "UPDATE"}, ForEachRow: true, Function: "kb_articles_tsv()",
	})
}
```

## Expressions

The builders live in the package `github.com/azrtydxb/momo/fts`. They used to be
functions of the root package; see [upgrading](upgrading.md) for
the name table.

The text search configuration (`english`, `simple`, ...) is a string. It is
bound as a parameter and cast to regconfig, so it cannot carry SQL; an empty
one fails the build with `ErrValidation`.

| Builder                | SQL                                            | Result type                |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `fts.TSMatch`          | `vec @@ query`                                 | `Predicate`                |
| `fts.TSVector`         | `to_tsvector(config, text)`                    | `fts.Expr[types.TSVector]` |
| `fts.TSWebsearchQuery` | `websearch_to_tsquery(config, text)`           | `fts.Expr[types.TSQuery]`  |
| `fts.TSPlainQuery`     | `plainto_tsquery(config, text)`                | `fts.Expr[types.TSQuery]`  |
| `fts.TSPhraseQuery`    | `phraseto_tsquery(config, text)`               | `fts.Expr[types.TSQuery]`  |
| `fts.TSQuery`          | `to_tsquery(config, text)`                     | `fts.Expr[types.TSQuery]`  |
| `fts.TSRank`           | `ts_rank(vec, query [, normalization])`        | `fts.Expr[float64]`        |
| `fts.TSRankCD`         | `ts_rank_cd(vec, query [, normalization])`     | `fts.Expr[float64]`        |
| `fts.TSHeadline`       | `ts_headline(config, text, query [, options])` | `fts.Expr[string]`         |

The query text, the configuration and the headline options are always bound
parameters. The normalization argument of the rank functions is the optional
PostgreSQL flag mask (0 to 63) and renders as a literal. `fts.TSWebsearchQuery`
accepts any user input without raising a syntax error, so it is the builder for
a search box; `fts.TSQuery` expects tsquery syntax and a malformed query is a
database error.

An `fts.Expr` has `As`, `Asc`, `Desc` and the comparison methods of any scalar
expression, so it works in Where, OrderBy and Columns:

<!-- docscheck:fragment -->

```go
q := fts.TSWebsearchQuery("english", userInput)
rank := fts.TSRankCD(articleSearch, q)

hits, err := momo.Select[Hit](db).
	From(momo.TableRef{Name: "kb_articles"}).
	Columns(articleID, rank.As("rank"),
		fts.TSHeadline("english", articleBody, q, "StartSel=<b>, StopSel=</b>, MaxFragments=2")).
	Where(fts.TSMatch(articleSearch, q)).
	OrderBy(rank.Desc()).
	Limit(20).
	All(ctx)
```

Here `articleSearch` is a `Column[types.TSVector]` and `articleBody` a
`Column[string]`. Without a stored column, search a text column directly with
`fts.TSVector` over `articleBody` as the first operand of `fts.TSMatch` (an
expression index on the same expression keeps it fast).

Every use of a call binds its own parameters (the configuration and the query
text), so the same expression written in the select list and again in GROUP BY
gets different placeholders, and PostgreSQL rejects the statement as an
ungrouped column. The same applies to SELECT DISTINCT with an ORDER BY on the
call. Group by a stored tsvector instead, or compute the call once in a
subquery or CTE and refer to its alias. A golden test pins the placeholders.

Arguments bound by these calls are masked in hook events (shown as
`RedactedArg`) when an operand reads a column marked sensitive; the driver
still receives the real values.

## Hybrid ranking: vector plus text

For reciprocal rank fusion of the two signals, use `momo.HybridSearch` (see
[hybrid search](vectors.md#hybrid-search)). To weigh the signals yourself,
combine them in one score with the typed arithmetic helpers. The cosine
distance is lower for better matches and the text rank is higher, so subtract a
weighted rank from the distance and order ascending:

<!-- docscheck:fragment -->

```go
dist := vecop.Cosine(articleEmb, queryEmbedding) // vector.Vector
text := fts.TSRankCD(articleSearch, fts.TSWebsearchQuery("english", userInput))
score := sqlfn.SubExpr[float64](dist, sqlfn.Mul[float64](text, 0.5))

hits, err := momo.Select[Hit](db).
	From(momo.TableRef{Name: "kb_articles"}).
	Columns(articleID, score.As("score"), articleTitle).
	OrderBy(score.Asc()).
	Limit(20).
	All(ctx)
```

This scores every row. To restrict the candidate set to text matches, add
a Where on `fts.TSMatch` over `articleSearch` and the same query, which lets the GIN
index prune the rows before the vector distance is computed. The
`TestFullTextHybridRanking` integration test runs this pattern.

## Scanning

pgx returns tsvector and tsquery values as text, which `types.TSVector` and
`types.TSQuery` scan. `ts_rank` and `ts_rank_cd` return real; they scan into
`float64` fields.


# Source: mysql.md

# MySQL and MariaDB

What works on MySQL and MariaDB today, and what does not. The driver is
`driver/mysqldriver` (database/sql on `github.com/go-sql-driver/mysql`).
The migration dialect `migrate/mysql` runs from the `momo migrate` command
with `--dialect mysql` (see [Migrations](#migrations) and the generated status
in [capabilities](capabilities.md)).

## Supported servers

| Server           | Version | Image used in CI |
| ---------------- | ------- | ---------------- |
| MySQL 8.4 LTS    | 8.4.13  | `mysql:8.4.13`   |
| MySQL 9.7 LTS    | 9.7.4   | `mysql:9.7.4`    |
| MariaDB 11.8 LTS | 11.8.9  | `mariadb:11.8.9` |

No innovation releases are supported. CI runs the shared suites against all
three servers (the `integration-mysql` job), on every push.

## What runs on a real server

The `integration-mysql` CI job starts one server per row of the table above and
runs the whole integration suite against it with `MOMO_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1`,
so a server that is missing fails the job instead of skipping the tests.
Tests that use `testopen.EachWithMySQL` or `testopen.EachMySQL` run on all
three servers; the plain `testopen.Each` opens PostgreSQL and SQLite only.

Run on MySQL 8.4, MySQL 9.7 and MariaDB 11.8:

- the shared suites: transactions, errors, joins, aggregates, subqueries and
  CTEs, RETURNING, raw SQL, locking, hints, keyset pagination, writes, soft
  delete, optimistic lock, upserts and timestamps;
- `jsonop.Text`, `jsonop.Path`, `jsonop.Root`, `jsonop.Contains`,
  `jsonop.HasKey` and `jsonop.DeleteKey`, with the build error of
  `jsonop.Concat` and `jsonop.Set`;
- window functions (ranking, `Lag`, `Lead`, `FirstValue`, `LastValue`, `Rows`
  and `Range` frames), the build error for a `Groups` frame, the aggregate
  `FILTER` clause (rewritten to `CASE WHEN`, with and without `Over` and in
  `HAVING`), and `LoadPerParentLimit`;
- keyset pagination over string, descending and mixed keys, `Batches`, and
  `SelectQuery.Each` and `SelectQuery.Iter`, including an early stop, a query
  while the cursor is open, a canceled context and a stream inside a `Tx`;
- typed predicates, row-value comparison, projections, select-list aliases,
  the `sqlfn` string, CASE, cast and arithmetic helpers, `timeop.CurrentDate`,
  the `agg` aggregates and bulk-insert chunking with `WithMaxParams`;
- every `timeop` extract field, truncation unit and interval, `timeop.Now`,
  `timeop.EpochSeconds` and the typed date arithmetic.

`LATERAL` runs on MySQL 8.4 and 9.7, and on MariaDB it is `ErrUnsupported`.
`CreateGraph` and `FindOrCreate` work on all three (see below), and a test
checks the stored keys and the found and created cases on each server.
`SelectQuery.Explain`, the aggregate `FILTER` clause on `agg.JSONB`,
`agg.Array`, an ordered or distinct `agg.JSONB`, `unnest` and `generate_series` sources are `ErrUnsupported`;
the tests check the error on each server. `DistinctOn` is emulated with
`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` in a derived table. A nullable model or
`NullColumn` `OrderBy` item with no NULLS term gets PostgreSQL's placement
(ASC last, DESC first), so the rows match; give a `ColumnOf` or expression item
an explicit `NullsFirst` or `NullsLast`. A subquery or CTE that reads an
unaliased expression by its PostgreSQL name must alias it, because it is
`momo_cN` here. Combined with a row lock it is `ErrUnsupported`.

Differences the tests pin down:

- a JSON null member extracts as the text `null`, not as SQL NULL, because
  `JSON_UNQUOTE` turns it into text;
- `sqlfn.Cast` writes the type name as given, and MySQL and MariaDB cast to
  `SIGNED`, not `bigint`;
- `momo.MapRows` returns text columns as `[]byte`, the driver's own type;
- an aggregate over `JSON_ARRAYAGG` has no defined member order.

Not run on MySQL or MariaDB: the one-million-row heap bound of streaming
(its seed SQL is PostgreSQL and SQLite only), and the CreateGraph behaviour
tests of the shared suite whose SQL is written for PostgreSQL alone. The graph writes
have their own tests in `driver/mysqldriver` and `rel_mysql_integration_test.go`.

## Connecting

Open the pool with `mysqldriver.Open(ctx, dsn, opts...)`, which returns a driver
that owns the pool (`db.Close()` closes it), or build
the DSN with `mysqldriver.ConfigureDSN` and pass the `*sql.DB` you opened to
`mysqldriver.New(db, opts...)`, which never closes it. The flavor is the option
`mysqldriver.WithFlavor`: `dialect.FlavorMySQL` (the default) or
`dialect.FlavorMariaDB`. The configured DSN always has:

- `parseTime=true` and `loc=UTC`, and the session `time_zone` set to `+00:00`;
- `clientFoundRows=true`, so an UPDATE reports the rows it matched;
- `interpolateParams=false` and `multiStatements=false`: values always travel
  as bound parameters of a prepared statement and never become SQL text. A DSN
  that sets either is overridden. A `*sql.DB` handed to `New` directly must
  already be configured this way.

`Open` pings the server, as the SQLite drivers do, so a bad DSN, a refused
connection or bad credentials fail at `Open` and not on the first statement.
An unknown flavor makes `Open` return `ErrUnsupported`; on any error the pool
is closed and nothing is returned. (`New`, which takes an already opened
`*sql.DB`, still returns a driver whose every call is `ErrUnsupported` for an
unknown flavor, because it has no error to return.) The `Open` of an earlier
release took the flavor as an argument and returned the `*sql.DB` too; see
[upgrading](upgrading.md).

`ConfigureDSN` (and so `Open`) refuses two DSN settings with `ErrValidation`:

- `allowAllFiles=true`, which lets the server read any client file through
  `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE`;
- `allowCleartextPasswords=true`, which sends the password unhashed.

Remove them from the DSN. The error message never quotes the DSN.

Transport security is the DSN's business and defaults to none: add `tls=true`
(or a registered TLS config) for any server that is not on the same host.

## Capabilities

The rows below are checked against `dialect.MySQLFlavor` by
`TestCapabilityMatrixMatchesDialect`.

| Capability       | mysql | mariadb    |
| ---------------- | ----- | ---------- |
| Returning        | no    | no         |
| InsertReturning  | no    | yes        |
| DeleteReturning  | no    | yes        |
| OnConflict       | no    | no         |
| OnDuplicateKey   | yes   | yes        |
| NullsOrdering    | no    | no         |
| TransactionalDDL | no    | no         |
| Merge            | no    | no         |
| ILike            | no    | no         |
| Locking          | yes   | yes        |
| RowValues        | yes   | yes        |
| Savepoints       | yes   | yes        |
| Vector.Storage   | yes   | yes        |
| Vector.Metrics   | none  | l2, cosine |
| Vector.Indexes   | none  | vector     |

`NullsOrdering`, `ILike` and `Merge` mean native syntax, not availability. All
three work on MySQL and MariaDB through emulation (see
[Emulated features](#emulated-features)), so the table says `no` while
`momo.ILike`, `NullsFirst`, `NullsLast` and `momo.Merge` run.

`Returning` is the form every statement has. MariaDB returns rows from an
INSERT (`InsertReturning`, 10.5 or later) and from a single-table DELETE
(`DeleteReturning`, 10.0.5 or later), but not from an UPDATE, which is why
`Returning` stays false: `Returning` on an insert or a delete works on MariaDB,
and on an update it is `ErrUnsupported` on both servers. A `Delete` with
`Using` is a multi-table DELETE, which MariaDB refuses with `RETURNING`, so
that combination is `ErrUnsupported` too. MySQL has no `RETURNING` at all; the
error for a delete names MariaDB as the alternative.

## Emulated features

Four PostgreSQL features have no MySQL or MariaDB spelling. Momo renders an
equivalent instead of returning `ErrUnsupported`.

- **ILIKE.** `momo.ILike(col, pattern)` renders
  `LOWER(col) LIKE LOWER(?) ESCAPE '!'`, and `momo.Not(momo.ILike(...))` negates
  it. `LOWER` folds Unicode letters by the character set, but the `LIKE`
  comparison follows the column collation. The default collations of MySQL 8.4
  and 9.7 (`utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci`) and MariaDB 11.8 are accent-insensitive, so `a`
  matches `ä`, which PostgreSQL `ILIKE` does not. Momo does not force a
  collation, because the accent-insensitive `_ai_` family is the thing it must
  not add. Because `LOWER` wraps the column, an index on the column is not
  used. The column must be a character type: on `BINARY`, `VARBINARY` and `BLOB`
  columns `LOWER` does nothing and `LIKE` is case-sensitive, so the match is
  case-sensitive there (momo adds no `CONVERT`).
- **NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST.** `NullsFirst` renders
  `(e IS NULL) DESC, e ASC|DESC` and `NullsLast` renders
  `(e IS NULL) ASC, e ASC|DESC`, which orders exactly as PostgreSQL. `e` is
  rendered twice, so values it binds appear twice among the arguments, in
  order. `After` over a nullable key stays `ErrUnsupported`, and the outer
  `OrderBy` of a union with a NULLS term is `ErrUnsupported`, and so is a window
  with a `Range` frame that has an offset and a single `OrderBy` item with a
  NULLS term (the emulation adds a second sort key, and the server rejects that
  with error 3587).
- **Aggregate FILTER.** `agg(x) FILTER (WHERE p)` renders
  `agg(CASE WHEN p THEN x END)`, and `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p)` renders
  `COUNT(CASE WHEN p THEN 1 END)`. It is exact for `Sum`, `Avg`, `Min`, `Max`,
  `CountOf`, `CountDistinct` and `agg.String`, and works with `Over`. A call
  that keeps NULLs (`agg.JSONB`, any `agg.Func` outside `count`, `sum`, `avg`,
  `min`, `max` and the `std` and `var` family, or one over a raw `*`) stays
  `ErrUnsupported`; use `momo.CountAll().Filter(p)` for `COUNT(*)`.
- **MERGE.** `momo.Merge` has no MySQL or MariaDB spelling, so `Exec` runs a
  sequence in one transaction (a savepoint inside a `Tx`). It copies the source
  into a temporary table, creates a second temporary table of the (target row,
  source row) pairs that `On` joins, read with `FOR UPDATE` so the matched
  target rows are locked and read at their latest committed version, checks
  that no target row is matched by two source rows (`ErrTooManyRows`), runs the
  multi-table `UPDATE target, pairs AS n SET target.c = n.v0 ...`, runs an
  `INSERT ... SELECT` of the source rows that have no pair, and drops both
  tables. Every new value is computed into the pairs table from the row as it
  was before the statement, because a multi-table `UPDATE` assigns left to
  right and `SET a = x, b = target.a` would otherwise read the new `a`; the
  match is decided before any write, so the result matches PostgreSQL even when
  the update changes a column that `On` reads. `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` is not
  used: it matches on any unique key, not on `On`. Not equivalent under
  concurrent writers: a row committed between the steps that starts to match is
  not seen (no gap or phantom protection, under repeatable read or read
  committed), and the affected-row count is taken before the `UPDATE`; see
  [capabilities](capabilities.md#merge-on-sqlite-mysql-and-mariadb). The account
  needs the `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLES` privilege. The temporary tables take the
  column types and collations the server derives for them, so a source built
  from literals or bind parameters can meet a different collation than the
  target column, and the comparison then fails with an error (read the source
  from a table, or cast it); a source with duplicate column names (a join
  selecting `a.id` and `b.id`) fails, so alias them. A server with
  `enforce_gtid_consistency` on refuses `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE` inside a
  transaction when `binlog_format` is `STATEMENT` or `MIXED` (and older MySQL
  servers refuse it whatever the format); the error reaches you and nothing is
  written. `Returning` is `ErrUnsupported`. Read the statements with
  `MergeQuery.Statements`. MySQL does not roll a temporary table back, so the
  sequence drops both itself, also after a failure; a canceled context or a
  lost connection can leave them on that pooled connection until its next
  `Merge`, which drops them first.

## Writes

- A single `Model` insert reads `LAST_INSERT_ID` and writes it into the
  identity field of the model. A key generated on the Go side (an id
  generator) always wins; `LAST_INSERT_ID` is read only for a key the database
  generates. A plain multi-row `Models` insert through `Exec` returns and
  writes back no keys, because the ids of a multi-row statement depend on
  `innodb_autoinc_lock_mode`. On MariaDB, ask for them with `Returning`; on
  MySQL that is `ErrUnsupported`. The `LAST_INSERT_ID` write-back does not
  apply to an upsert or to any insert with a conflict clause
  (`wantsGeneratedKey` in the core is false for them), because the statement
  may update an existing row and `LAST_INSERT_ID` then does not name the row's
  key; read the row back with a query.
- `momo.CreateGraph` reads every generated key back on both servers. MariaDB
  uses `INSERT ... RETURNING` (`InsertReturning`), also for the children of a
  has-many or many-to-many relation, in one multi-row statement. MySQL has no
  `RETURNING`, so it reads `LAST_INSERT_ID` after each statement and inserts
  the children one row per statement inside the graph's transaction (a
  savepoint on a `Tx`). The keys of one multi-row `INSERT` are consecutive only
  when `innodb_autoinc_lock_mode` is 0 or 1; MySQL 8 and 9 default to 2, where
  concurrent inserts can interleave, so momo never infers keys from a
  multi-row statement and an `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` statement is never used
  to read keys. The rows share one statement clock, so they get the same
  automatic timestamps as a bulk insert. Children that mix zero and explicit
  keys in one bulk insert fail with `ErrValidation` on MySQL, and a generated
  key on a non-integer field is `ErrUnsupported`. CI runs this on MySQL 8.4 and
  9.7 (mode 2) and MariaDB 11.8.
- `momo.FindOrCreate` works on both servers inside a transaction (a savepoint
  on a `Tx`): a plain `INSERT` (with `RETURNING` on MariaDB, `LAST_INSERT_ID`
  on MySQL), and when it fails with a unique violation, a shared-lock select
  by key (`FOR SHARE`, `LOCK IN SHARE MODE` on MariaDB) that returns the stored
  row, so the Go-side key still wins for a new row. A no-op
  `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` cannot be used: with `clientFoundRows` an inserted
  row and an untouched existing row both report one affected row, and MariaDB's
  `RETURNING` returns the row either way, so `created` could not be told. The
  price is one failed `INSERT` plus one `SELECT` when the row exists, and the
  failed insert uses up an auto-increment value. Shared locks do not conflict
  with each other, but if the first inserter rolls back instead of committing,
  the waiting callers can deadlock (error 1213, `ErrSerialization`) and one
  retries. On a caller's `Tx`, InnoDB keeps the locks taken after a savepoint
  until the outer transaction ends. A unique violation on another
  key than the one given is still `ErrUniqueViolation`; a `DB` pinned with
  `OnConn` is `ErrUnsupported` (it cannot open the transaction).
- Upserts render as `INSERT ... VALUES ... AS momo_new ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`
  on MySQL and with `VALUES(col)` on MariaDB. A `FromSelect` upsert has no row
  alias on either: MySQL and MariaDB both render `VALUES(col)` there. The
  `updated_at` bump of a `DoUpdate` is a bound clock value, so it needs neither
  form. `DoNothing` renders a no-op
  assignment of a key column. A `Where` on a conflict clause is
  `ErrUnsupported`.
- `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` fires for a conflict on any unique key and cannot
  name one. Momo therefore accepts a conflict target only when it is a unique
  key of the table and no other unique key can conflict. A second key is safe
  when it is made only of auto-increment columns the insert leaves to the
  database: the server gives such a column a fresh value, so the key cannot
  match an existing row. The case this allows is an auto-increment primary key
  next to `UNIQUE(email)`, upserting on `email` with the primary key left out
  (judged from the columns the statement writes: the identity is not in the
  model columns, the `InsertQuery.Values` assignments or the `FromSelect`
  target list, and no Go-side id generator fills it). In every other case the call is `ErrUnsupported` and the message
  names the reason: a second unique key the insert can reach (an ordinary
  column, an expression, a composite key with an ordinary column, or the
  primary key written explicitly), or a target that is not a unique key. The
  unique keys come from the model's schema (its `pk` and `unique` tags and
  unique indexes); without a schema (a hand-written model) only a primary-key
  target is accepted.
- With `clientFoundRows`, an upsert reports 1 for an inserted row, 2 for an
  existing row that changed, and 1 for an existing row set to its current
  values. `DoNothing` also reports 1 for a skipped row. A count of 1 does not
  tell an insert from a skip.
- `BulkUpdate` and `BulkUpdateKeys` render
  `UPDATE t JOIN (SELECT k, c FROM t WHERE false UNION ALL SELECT ?, ? ...) AS momo_v ON t.k = momo_v.k SET t.c = momo_v.c`
  on both servers, because MariaDB has no `VALUES ROW(...)` table constructor.
  The empty first `SELECT` gives the rows the column types and collation of the
  table. A derived table with a `UNION` is materialized, so the server accepts
  the update of a table that the derived table also reads. `RowsAffected` counts
  the rows that match a listed key, changed or not, because the driver sets
  `clientFoundRows`. `Returning` is `ErrUnsupported`, as for any UPDATE. A list
  over `MaxParams` is split into chunks that run in one transaction (a
  savepoint on a `Tx`).
- A bare `OFFSET` gets `LIMIT 18446744073709551615` in front of it, because
  MySQL and MariaDB reject an offset without a limit.

## Locking and transactions

`ForUpdate` and `ForShare` render `FOR UPDATE` and `FOR SHARE`; `NOWAIT` and
`SKIP LOCKED` are passed through. MariaDB 11.8 has no `FOR SHARE`, so it gets
`LOCK IN SHARE MODE`. `LockOf` (`FOR UPDATE OF`) is MySQL only; on MariaDB it is
`ErrUnsupported`. Savepoints and the four standard isolation levels work;
read-only transactions use `START TRANSACTION READ ONLY`. Any other isolation
level is `ErrUnsupported`. `ForNoKeyUpdate` and `ForKeyShare` are PostgreSQL
only and return `ErrUnsupported` here. `timeop.ClockTimestamp` renders
`SYSDATE(6)`; `timeop.StatementTimestamp` is `ErrUnsupported`.

### Advisory locks

The `advisory` session functions `advisory.Acquire` and `advisory.Release`, with
`advisory.Try` for the non-blocking form and an `int64` or a string key, run on
MySQL and MariaDB with `GET_LOCK`, `GET_LOCK(name, 0)` and `RELEASE_LOCK`. A
`GET_LOCK` lock belongs to the connection, so pass a `*momo.DB` from
`db.OnConn(pc)` over a pinned connection (`pc` from `momo.Pinner`), exactly as
on PostgreSQL, and release the lock before you return the pinned connection to
the pool. A pooled `*momo.DB` is
`ErrValidation`.

- Key mapping: the lock name is `momo:advisory:<db>:<key>`. `GET_LOCK` names are
  global to the server, while a PostgreSQL advisory lock belongs to one
  database, so the name carries the current database as on PostgreSQL: `<db>` is
  the first 8 hex digits of `sha256(DATABASE())`, or `nodb` on a connection with
  no default database, read by the server on each call (a `USE` statement moves
  the connection to another lock space). `<key>` is the decimal `int64` key (for
  example `-42`) or `s:` plus the first 32 hex digits of the sha256 of a text key.
  The longest name is 57 characters, under the 64 that `GET_LOCK` allows.
  `advisory.WithHash64` has no effect, and a text key locks a different thing
  here than on PostgreSQL.
- `advisory.Acquire` with `advisory.Try` is `GET_LOCK(name, 0)`: `false` when
  another session holds the lock. A NULL result from the server is an error
  (`ErrBusy`). A key the same session already holds is granted at once and
  counted.
- `advisory.Acquire` without `advisory.Try` waits in one-second `GET_LOCK` calls
  until the lock is granted or the context ends, because a negative timeout waits
  forever on MySQL and returns NULL on MariaDB. A canceled context returns an
  `ErrCanceled` error that wraps the context error. After any `advisory.Acquire`
  error, `Discard` the pinned connection (`momo.Discarder`) instead of releasing
  it: a lock the server granted while the call was being abandoned may still be
  attached to the connection, and closing it frees the lock.
- `advisory.Release` is `RELEASE_LOCK`: `true` when this session held the lock,
  `false` for a lock another session holds or nobody holds. Locks are counted, so
  a key acquired twice needs two releases.
- `advisory.Xact` (the transaction-scoped lock) and `advisory.Shared` are
  `ErrUnsupported`. A `GET_LOCK` lock is not released by a commit or rollback and
  has no shared mode, so emulating them would silently hold a session lock.

## Errors

Server errors map by number: 1062 unique, 1451 and 1452 (and 1216, 1217)
foreign key, 1048 and 1364 not null, 3819 (MySQL) and 4025 (MariaDB) check,
1213 and MariaDB 1020 serialization (deadlock, and a row that changed under
`innodb_snapshot_isolation`), 1205 and 3572 busy. `Error()` never shows the
server text, which can quote a row value; `Detail()` returns it, and
`errors.As` reaches the `*mysql.MySQLError`. The constraint name differs by
server: MySQL 8 reports a unique key as `table.index`, MariaDB reports only the
index name.

## Vectors

MySQL 8.4 has no vector columns. MySQL 9.7 stores `VECTOR` and reads it back,
but offers no distance function in the Community edition (`DISTANCE()` is
HeatWave and MySQL AI only), so every distance builder is `ErrUnsupported` on
MySQL. MariaDB 11.8 renders `vecop.L2` as `VEC_DISTANCE_EUCLIDEAN` and
`vecop.Cosine` as `VEC_DISTANCE_COSINE` on `vector.Vector` columns, and its
driver reports `Vectors`. Inner product, L1, Hamming, Jaccard and the half,
sparse and bit types return `ErrUnsupported` on MariaDB. Details and the
`VECTOR INDEX` rules are in [vectors.md](vectors.md#mariadb-and-mysql).

## Migrations

The library dialect `migrate/mysql` inspects `information_schema`, renders DDL,
locks with `GET_LOCK` and runs every migration, up and down, statement by
statement, because DDL commits implicitly on these servers. Build the engine
with `migrate.WithDialect` and the `mysqldriver` driver; the inspector, drift
check and `-- momo:ddl` online DDL options work through it. The `momo migrate`
command does the same for you: `--dialect mysql`, with a `mysql://` or
`mariadb://` URL or a go-sql-driver DSN (one dialect for both servers; the
server tells them apart). A string without `size:N` is `text`, and `text`,
`blob` and `json` columns cannot be keyed: the generator refuses a model with
one in a primary key, unique key, index or foreign key, naming the column, so a
migration never fails half-way on error 1170. `types.Numeric` with a `precision`
tag is `decimal(p,s)` (precision up to 65, scale up to 30, scale not above
precision; no `NaN` or infinity), and a `vector.Vector` column is `vector(N)`,
which needs MySQL 9.0 or MariaDB 11.7. What the dialect reports and renders is in
[migrations.md](migrations.md#9-mysql-and-mariadb).

## Models from a database

`momo generate --from-db` reads a MySQL 8.4, MySQL 9.7 or MariaDB 11.8
database and writes the models and the init snapshot, as it does for
PostgreSQL. Set `dialects: [mysql]` in `momo.yaml` (MariaDB is the same
dialect; the flavor is read from the server). The command reuses the
`migrate/mysql` inspector, so what `momo migrate drift` sees is what the models
declare.

The value of `--from-db` is `-` for standard input, the name of an environment
variable that holds the connection, or the connection itself, in one of these
forms:

```text
user:pass@tcp(host:3306)/app          a go-sql-driver DSN
tcp(host:3306)/app                    the same without credentials
user:pass@unix(/run/mysqld.sock)/app  a unix socket (DSN only)
mysql://user:pass@host:3306/app       a URL, also mariadb://
```

The DSN must name the database. A URL may carry only `tls`, `timeout`,
`readTimeout`, `writeTimeout`, `charset`, `collation`, `maxAllowedPacket` and
`allowNativePasswords`; any other parameter is refused, because the server
would take it as a session variable. Use a DSN for sockets and every other
driver option. A DSN or URL for a remote host with no `tls=` setting prints a
warning, and the password, in either form, is redacted from every message.

## What a rebuilt database matches

A database rebuilt from the generated models (diff the models against an empty
database and apply) has the same schema as far as `schema.Equal` compares it:
columns, types, defaults, generated columns, keys, indexes, checks and foreign
keys. The `integration-mysql` jobs check that on all three servers with a
schema built from raw DDL. It is not byte for byte. These are known losses; the
ones the command can see are reported, the others are not:

```text
ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP   reported as a warning; the rebuilt column does not change on UPDATE
INVISIBLE columns             reported as a warning (MySQL); the rebuilt column is visible
prefix indexes, name(10)      reported as a warning; left out of the models and the snapshot
prefix PRIMARY KEY            an error: nothing is written
table charset and collation   not read; a column collation is read only where it differs from the table's
ENGINE, ROW_FORMAT, table comment, AUTO_INCREMENT counter, partitions   not read
triggers, views, stored routines                                         not read
```

Type mapping (the column type is always written as a `type:` tag, because the
generator has no MySQL type table, except `varchar(N)`, which becomes `size:N`):

```text
tinyint(1)                    bool (a pointer when nullable)
tinyint, smallint, mediumint  int8, int16, int32 (uint8, uint16, uint32 when unsigned)
int, bigint                   int32, int64 (uint32, uint64 when unsigned)
float, double                 float32, float64
decimal(p,s)                  types.Numeric
char, varchar, *text          string
binary, varbinary, *blob, bit []byte
date                          types.Date
datetime, timestamp           time.Time
time                          string (the driver returns TIME as text)
year                          int16
json                          types.JSON[json.RawMessage]
enum, set                     string
```

- **tinyint(1) is a Go bool.** MySQL stores any value from -128 to 127 in it,
  and a stored value other than 0 or 1 (a 2 written by another program) fails
  to scan, for the whole row. Every `tinyint(1)` column gets a note in the
  report. If the column holds other values, add an `introspect.types` rule that
  maps `tinyint(1)` to `int8`.
- **enum and set** are Go strings. The exact column type, values included, is
  written in the `type:` tag, so the database keeps the value list and a
  rebuilt database matches. No check constraint is added and the values are not
  checked in Go. The tag grammar reads a comma inside parentheses as part of
  the option and skips a quoted value there, so `type:decimal(10,2)` and
  `type:enum('a,b','it''s')` are one option each.
- **AUTO_INCREMENT** keys get the `identity` tag.
- **Defaults:** every default is written (`default:`). A NOT NULL `bool` or
  number column whose constant default is `true` or non-zero is handled by
  flavor, because only MariaDB has `INSERT ... RETURNING`. On MariaDB the field
  gets `dbdefault` and a pointer type, so nil takes the default and an explicit
  `false` or `0` is written. On MySQL 8.4 and 9.7 an insert that leaves a
  `dbdefault` field nil is refused (nothing reads the stored value back), so the
  field stays plain and the report has a note: a zero value is written instead
  of the column default. A computed default such as `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` gets no
  `dbdefault` on either.
- **Generated columns** become `read_only` fields with `generated:` (and
  `virtual` for VIRTUAL).
- **Constraints:** unique keys, plain, composite and `DESC` indexes, check
  constraints and foreign keys are written as on PostgreSQL. A foreign key to a
  primary key is a `belongs_to` field with `fk_name`, because MySQL names an
  unnamed key `<table>_ibfk_<n>`; `introspect.inverse` adds `has_many` and
  `has_one`. A foreign key to a unique column that is not the primary key is a
  `c.ForeignKey(...)` statement in `MomoConfig`, with no relation field.
- **Left out with a warning**, so the models and the snapshot agree and the
  baseline reports them: prefix indexes, foreign keys to a table with no model,
  and every object that PostgreSQL alone has (schemas, extensions, enum types,
  functions, triggers, row-level security, partitions), which MySQL does not
  have.
- **No Go mapping** (geometry, `vector`): an error, and nothing is written; add
  an `introspect.types` or `introspect.columns` rule.
- MariaDB stores `json` as `longtext` with a `json_valid` check; the inspector
  folds that back into `json`. MariaDB reports a literal default quoted and
  MySQL does not; both are written as the SQL literal.

# Migration safety and recovery

Momo v0.19.0, PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB (sections 3, 3a and 9). Every statement here was checked against <!-- x-release-please-version -->
`migrate/`, `cli/`, `schema/` and `dialect/`; the tests that pin a
behavior are named. For the first run see README, [Create and apply the
migration](../README.md#3-create-and-apply-the-migration).

`momo migrate` runs the PostgreSQL, SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB migration dialects
(`--dialect postgres`, `sqlite` or `mysql`). Apply semantics are in section 3
(PostgreSQL), section 3a (SQLite) and section 9 (MySQL and MariaDB):

<!-- generated:status -->

<!-- Generated by go generate ./internal/gendocs from the code. Do not edit by hand. -->

A database is usable when a driver package for it exists under `driver/`:

- PostgreSQL: usable through `driver/pgxdriver` (vector builders: yes). Migrations: `migrate/postgres`, run by `momo migrate`.
- SQLite: usable through `driver/sqlitedriver` (needs cgo, not on Windows, vector builders: yes) and `driver/sqlitepure` (vector builders: no). Migrations: `migrate/sqlite`, run by `momo migrate`.
- MySQL and MariaDB: usable through `driver/mysqldriver` (vector storage and builders depend on the server version). Migrations: `migrate/mysql`, run by `momo migrate`.

<!-- /generated:status -->

## 1. Model

```text
models (Go structs) --momo migrate diff--> <v>_<name>.up.sql + <v>_<name>.snapshot.json + momo.sum
                                              |
database <--------momo migrate apply---------+  (history table: momo_migrations)
```

### Files

All files live in one directory per dialect (default `migrations/postgres`,
set `migrate.dir.postgres` or `--dir`). `diff` writes exactly three files:

| File                             | Content                                                                                                                                                                        |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `<version>_<name>.up.sql`        | Statements. Header `-- momo:generated`, plus `-- momo:destructive` and/or `-- momo:no-transaction` when needed. Statements are separated by a blank line and each ends in `;`. |
| `<version>_<name>.snapshot.json` | The schema after this migration as `{format_version, version, parent, schema}`; `parent` is the migration it was generated from. `schema` has its own `format_version`.        |
| `momo.sum`                       | Checksum manifest of every file in the directory, one line per file, extended by `diff`.                                                                                       |

- `version` is a 14-digit UTC timestamp (`YYYYMMDDHHMMSS`). If the clock is not
  past the latest existing version, `diff` uses the second after it, so
  versions only grow.
- `name` must match `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$`.
- `.down.sql` files are optional and hand-written (`diff` never generates one).
  They are hashed in `momo.sum`, and `apply` never runs them. Only
  `Engine.Rollback` runs them (section 2).
- Files whose name starts with `.` are ignored everywhere (`.DS_Store`,
  `.momo-*.tmp`). A symlink to a directory inside the migration directory is an
  error. Moving an applied file into a subdirectory is fine: history is keyed by
  version, not path (`TestMovingAppliedMigrationIntoArchiveKeepsHistory`).
- `diff` never overwrites a file (exit 1 if one exists) and writes all-or-none:
  temporaries first, then publish, `momo.sum` last.

### Format versions

| Artifact         | Field                                 | v0.19.0 value | Newer than this binary <!-- x-release-please-version --> |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Snapshot wrapper | `format_version`                      | 1             | read error, "upgrade momo"                               |
| Embedded schema  | `schema.format_version`               | 1             | read error, "upgrade momo"                               |
| `momo.sum`       | header `# momo.sum format=N`          | 2 (reads 1)   | `migrate.ErrNewerFormat`                                 |
| History table    | `checksum` of the row `__momo_meta__` | 1             | apply refuses, "upgrade momo"                            |

A snapshot without `format_version` is rejected.

Adding the optional column field `generated_virtual` (a VIRTUAL generated
column on MySQL and SQLite) did not bump `format_version`: a snapshot without
it loads and its generated columns are STORED.

The same holds for the optional `sequences` key, the standalone PostgreSQL
sequences (section 7): a snapshot without it loads with none, and the format
version stays the same. A momo release that predates the key reads a snapshot
that has it without an error and ignores the sequences, so it plans neither
their creation nor their drop and reports no drift for them. Read and write
snapshots with one momo release.

### Diff

`momo migrate diff <name>` runs offline (no database, no driver). It loads the
models, compares them with the schema after the latest migration in the
directory (the snapshot of the highest version, or after a merge of branches
the derived schema described under Parallel branches; the empty schema when
there is none), orders the changes by
dependency and renders SQL. No difference: prints `no changes`, exit 0, writes
nothing.

- Renames are never guessed. A drop plus an add prints a
  `hint: possible rename ...`; pass `--rename-table old=new` or
  `--rename-column table.old=new`.
- Dropped extensions and schemas are not dropped in the database; `diff` prints
  a hint that they are no longer managed.
- Diff never reads the database. A table that is already populated is
  indistinguishable from an empty one (see section 5).

`diff` does not depend on `momo generate`. `momo generate --check` verifies only
the generated `*_gen.go` files (exit 1 and `stale: <path>` lines when stale).
There is no `momo migrate diff --check`. To fail CI when the models have no
migration, run `momo migrate diff ci_probe` on a clean checkout and fail unless
it prints `no changes` (when there is a difference it writes files and exits 0,
so also check `git status --porcelain` on the migration directory). This recipe
is derived from the code, not covered by a test.

### Value-list checks

A check declared with `Config.CheckIn` restricts a string field to a list of
values. The snapshot keeps the list next to the expression (`schema.Check.In`,
a `schema.CheckIn` with the column and the values, sorted and without
duplicates), so `diff` compares two lists of the same name and column as sets
of values:

- The same set of values in another order, or with a value repeated, is no
  change.
- A different set is one `migrate.AlterCheckIn` change that carries the
  `migrate.Change.Added` and `migrate.Change.Removed` values, in place of the drop and add of a whole
  constraint that an ordinary `Config.Check` gets.
- A removed value is destructive: `diff` refuses it without
  `--allow-destructive`, prints `backfill rows holding 'x' first`, and writes
  `-- momo:destructive` to the migration. The new constraint rejects every row
  that still holds the value, so backfill them in an earlier migration. The
  lint rule `check-value-removal` reports a migration that removes a value
  without the directive.

Each value is on its own source line, so two branches that add different
values to one list merge as text; at most the two lines are inserted in the
same place, and keeping both resolves it. Diff the merged declaration to get
one migration that adds both values. Two migrations that each carry one branch's
change cannot be applied in either order and keep both values, because a
migration restates the whole list: generate one migration after the merge, or
regenerate with `momo migrate rebase`.

What the migration does on each dialect:

- PostgreSQL: `DROP CONSTRAINT` and `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID` in the
  transactional file, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` in the `_no_tx` file. The table
  is never without a constraint, and the validation scan runs outside the lock
  of the change.
- SQLite: a table rebuild that recreates the table with the new CHECK. A removed
  value that rows still hold fails the copy, and the transaction rolls back.
- MySQL 8.4, MySQL 9.7 and MariaDB 11.8: one
  `ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT ck, ADD CONSTRAINT ck CHECK (...)`, so the
  table is never without the constraint. All three enforce CHECK constraints, and
  they accept `DROP CONSTRAINT` for one (older MySQL releases parse and ignore
  CHECK, or spell the drop `DROP CHECK`). A removed value that rows hold makes
  the statement fail.

The expression is `"col" IN ('a','b')` (backticks on MySQL and MariaDB) with
the values sorted. Drift reads the list out of the stored expression and
compares it as a set with the snapshot's, so another quoting or order of the
same values is not drift. `momo generate --from-db` reads a constraint
over one text column that has this shape and writes it as a `Config.CheckIn`
declaration, one sorted value per line. On SQLite a constraint that has a name
is a declared check, and only an unnamed CHECK over a TEXT column is read as an
enum column. A list needs a text column: an enum column, a column of another
type, an empty list, and a value that holds a backslash or a control character
are refused.

### Deferrable constraints

A unique constraint, a primary key and a foreign key can be `DEFERRABLE` or
`DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` on PostgreSQL: the transaction checks the
constraint at commit, so it can move rows through a state that would collide
(reordering the rows of a list under `UNIQUE (route_id, position)` is the usual
case). The model keeps two flags per constraint: `schema.Unique.Deferrable` and
`schema.Unique.InitiallyDeferred`, the same pair on `schema.ForeignKey`, and
`schema.Table.PrimaryKeyDeferrable` and `schema.Table.PrimaryKeyInitiallyDeferred`
for the primary key. `INITIALLY DEFERRED` implies `DEFERRABLE`, so the two
spellings of an initially deferred constraint compare equal. A snapshot written
before the flags existed loads with none of them set, which is `NOT DEFERRABLE`,
so the snapshot format version stays 1 and no snapshot needs rewriting.

The declaration is read from `MomoConfig`:

- `Config.Unique` takes `IndexOpts.Deferrable` or `IndexOpts.InitiallyDeferred`.
  A deferrable unique stays a constraint, so it takes no other option:
  `IndexOpts.Where`, `IndexOpts.Method`, `IndexOpts.With`, `IndexOpts.Opclass`,
  `IndexOpts.Desc`, `IndexOpts.Nulls`, `IndexOpts.Concurrently` or
  `IndexOpts.Unique` makes it an index, which PostgreSQL cannot defer, and the
  generator refuses the combination. `Config.Index` and `Config.IndexExpr` refuse
  both options.
- `Config.ForeignKey` takes `ForeignKeyOpts.Deferrable` or
  `ForeignKeyOpts.InitiallyDeferred`. A `belongs_to` tag has no such option, so
  declare a deferrable key with `Config.ForeignKey`.
- `Config.PrimaryKeyDeferrable` and `Config.PrimaryKeyInitiallyDeferred` mark
  the primary key; the model must have one.

SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB cannot model them. MySQL and MariaDB check every
constraint at the end of the statement and have no `DEFERRABLE`. SQLite defers
a foreign key only, and `PRAGMA foreign_key_list` does not report that, so momo
could not read a declared flag back and every inspection would differ from the
model. The generator reports a diagnostic for a deferrable constraint when the
target dialect is not PostgreSQL, and the SQLite and MySQL renderers return an
error that wraps `momo.ErrUnsupported`.

A foreign key cannot reference a deferrable primary key or a deferrable unique
constraint. PostgreSQL refuses to create it (`cannot use a deferrable unique
constraint for referenced table`), so a table that other tables reference, with
`belongs_to` or `Config.ForeignKey`, keeps an immediate key. The generator
reports a diagnostic that names the foreign key and the deferrable key it
references, and `migrate.Diff` returns an error with the same names before it plans a
change, so the migration never fails half way through. A column set that a
non-deferrable key also covers is accepted: PostgreSQL uses that key. Make the
referenced key immediate, or have the foreign key reference a column set that
an immediate unique constraint or unique index covers. The deferrable foreign
key itself, and a deferrable key that nothing references, are fine.

What the tools do on PostgreSQL:

- `momo generate --from-db` reads `pg_constraint.condeferrable` and
  `condeferred` and writes the declarations above; a deferrable foreign key is
  written as `Config.ForeignKey`, because the tag form cannot say it. A database
  built from the generated init migration recreates the constraints deferrable.
- `diff` renders `DEFERRABLE` or `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` after the
  constraint in `CREATE TABLE` and `ADD CONSTRAINT` (a unique added to an
  existing table keeps the concurrent index build, and the flags go on the
  `ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX` statement).
- A change of deferrability is a change of the constraint: `diff` drops it and
  adds it again, like any other change of a constraint, in one transaction.
  PostgreSQL has `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER CONSTRAINT` for a foreign key, but
  not for a unique constraint or a primary key, so one rule covers all three.
  Re-adding a foreign key validates the table again. A primary key or unique
  constraint that a foreign key references is never deferrable (see the limit
  below), so `diff` never has to drop one to change its deferrability: the
  desired schema is refused before any statement is planned.
- `Baseline`, `drift` and `drift --fix-sql` compare the flags with the other
  attributes. A difference reads `deferrable=false` on one side and
  `deferrable=true` on the other, and the repair is the drop and add above. As
  every drop, it is withheld unless `--allow-destructive` is given.

### Exclusion constraints

An exclusion constraint on PostgreSQL forbids two rows from satisfying every
operator of the constraint at once: `EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during
WITH &&)` stops two bookings of one room from overlapping, which a unique
constraint cannot say. The model keeps them in `schema.Table.Excludes`, each a
`schema.Exclude` with a name, an access method (`gist` when empty, and a
normalized schema always says it), a list of `schema.ExcludeElement` (a column
and an operator) and the same `Deferrable` and `InitiallyDeferred` flags as a
unique constraint. A snapshot written before they existed loads with none, so
the snapshot format version stays 1.

The declaration is `Config.Exclude` in `MomoConfig`: a name, then pairs of a
field reference and the operator, with `ExcludeOpts.Using`,
`ExcludeOpts.Deferrable` and `ExcludeOpts.InitiallyDeferred` to chain. For
the bookings above it is `c.Exclude("bookings_no_overlap", &b.RoomID, "=", &b.During,
"&&")`. The operator is a string literal of operator characters and is checked before
it reaches a statement. The constraint is backed by an index of its own name, so
it shares the index namespace and the generator refuses a name that an index or
a unique constraint already has. A GiST index over a scalar column such as
`room_id` needs the `btree_gist` extension; the generator adds it to the schema
when a constraint compares a scalar, so a migration creates it before the table.
A constraint over range columns alone needs none. SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB
have no exclusion constraints: the generator reports a diagnostic for a
declaration when the target dialect is not PostgreSQL, and the SQLite and MySQL
renderers return an error that wraps `momo.ErrUnsupported`.

Only plain columns with their default operator class and ordering are modelled:
an expression, a `WHERE` predicate, an `INCLUDE` list, an operator class, an
ordering and storage parameters are not. The PostgreSQL inspector reads each
constraint from `pg_get_constraintdef`, and refuses one it cannot model with an
error that names the constraint and its table, because skipping it would let
`Baseline` and `drift` call a database clean that does not match its model.
Hide the table with `migrate.exclude` to proceed, and keep that constraint in a
migration written by hand.

What the tools do on PostgreSQL:

- `momo generate --from-db` writes `Config.Exclude` for each inspected
  constraint, with `Using` for a method other than `gist` and the deferral
  calls. A range column comes out as a `types.Range` field.
- `diff` renders the constraint after the unique constraints in `CREATE TABLE`,
  and as an `ADD CONSTRAINT` and a `DROP CONSTRAINT` statement on an existing
  table. Any change of the elements, the method or the deferrability is a drop
  and an add of the constraint in one transaction, because PostgreSQL cannot
  alter one. Adding one to a table that holds rows
  builds a GiST index and checks every row under an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, and
  fails if existing rows already conflict; `diff` reports it as a risky change.
- `Baseline`, `drift` and `drift --fix-sql` compare each constraint as an object
  of its table. A constraint that is missing, extra or different is reported,
  and the repair is the drop and add above, withheld without
  `--allow-destructive` like every drop. `AutoMigrate` never drops one.

### Checksums

Two independent checks, both SHA-256 of the file bytes:

1. `momo.sum` must match the directory: every file present, none added,
   removed or changed. `Engine.Apply`, `Status` and `Baseline` refuse otherwise
   (`ErrChecksumMismatch`, naming the files). A missing `momo.sum` is an error
   that names `momo migrate hash`.
   `momo.sum` format 2 is the header `# momo.sum format=2` and one
   `<sha256>  <file name>` line per file, in any order (`hash` and `diff` write
   them sorted). It has no directory hash, so a line that is not a checksum
   line, such as a leftover conflict marker, is rejected, and so is a file name
   listed with two different checksums. Format 1, which has an `h1:`
   directory-hash line after the header, is still read and still rejects a
   hand-edit that left the hash stale. `diff` and `new --custom` keep the format
   of the `momo.sum` they extend; `momo migrate hash` writes format 2, which
   upgrades a format 1 file, and `momo migrate hash --sum-format 1` writes
   format 1 again. A momo that predates format 2 stops at the header with
   `migrate.ErrNewerFormat`, so it never misreads the file.
2. The history row of an applied migration stores the checksum of its up file.
   `Engine.Apply` refuses when that file changed since (the error says
   `... changed after version V was applied`).

`Plan` and `Drift` do not check either.

### History table

`momo_migrations`. Every statement against it (read, insert, update, delete
and the `CREATE TABLE`) names the table schema-qualified and quoted, for
example `"app"."momo_migrations"`. The table is resolved before the lock is
taken, and again right after, and the advisory-lock key is built from that
resolved schema, so a migration that changes `search_path` cannot redirect the
history writes. If the two lookups disagree (another process created the table
in an earlier schema in between), the lock is released and the attempt is
repeated once; a second disagreement fails with an error asking you to retry.

- An existing table is found the way earlier versions found it, through the
  session `search_path`, and its schema is then used. Installs made with the
  unqualified name keep working, and no second table is created.
- `postgres.New(postgres.WithHistorySchema("app"))` skips that search: the table
  is looked up as `"app".momo_migrations` and a new one is created in `app`,
  whatever else is on the `search_path`. `momotest` uses it so a test schema
  gets its own history even when `public` holds a `momo_migrations`.
- The resolved object must be a regular, permanent table, and the connecting
  role must be its owner or hold the privileges of the owning role
  (`pg_has_role` with `USAGE`, so a role with NOINHERIT does not qualify). A
  superuser holds every role's privileges, so a superuser migrator
  additionally requires the owner to be itself or another superuser; a table
  owned by an ordinary role is refused, because its triggers and rules would
  run with superuser rights. A view, foreign table, unlogged or temporary table, or a table
  owned by an unrelated role, named `momo_migrations` earlier on the
  `search_path`, is refused with a validation error naming the schema, the
  table and the owner; it is never used. A table adopted on first install by
  `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` passes the same checks after the statement runs.
- What this does and does not defend: it stops a foreign-owned or non-table
  object that sits ahead of the real table on the `search_path` from
  capturing the history writes. It does not stop a role whose privileges you hold,
  or another superuser, from owning such an object, and it cannot protect a schema
  that other roles may write to and that is ahead of yours on the
  `search_path` before any table exists. Keep schemas on the migrator's
  `search_path` writable only by the migrator.
- With no table yet, it is created in the current schema.
  `migrate.Settings.Schemas[0]` (`migrate.schemas`) must equal the current schema
  (current_schema) or the engine returns a configuration error naming both.
  `plan`, `status` and `drift` on a connection with no current schema and no
  table report an empty history; `apply` and the other writers fail.
- momo does not `SET search_path` for the migration session. Migrations are
  written against the `search_path` of the connection you give momo and may
  rely on it; qualify the history table, not the migrations. Set the
  `search_path` in the connection URL, and pin it per role with
  `ALTER ROLE` on the migrator role.

| Column               | Type             | Meaning                                                                                   |
| -------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `version`            | TEXT PRIMARY KEY | Migration version                                                                         |
| `name`               | TEXT             | Migration name                                                                            |
| `checksum`           | TEXT             | SHA-256 of the up file                                                                    |
| `status`             | TEXT             | `running`, `applied`, `failed`, `rolled_back` (and `meta`)                                |
| `statements_applied` | INTEGER          | Statements that completed                                                                 |
| `error`              | TEXT             | Failure text, empty on success                                                            |
| `applied_at`         | TEXT             | RFC 3339 UTC                                                                              |
| `execution_ms`       | BIGINT           | Duration                                                                                  |
| `apply_id`           | TEXT             | UTC timestamp plus 8 hex digits, shared by one `apply` run; `baseline` for baselined rows |
| `kind`               | TEXT             | `sql` (default), or `go` for a Go migration (section 6a)                                  |

One extra row, `version = '__momo_meta__'`, `status = 'meta'`, holds the
history format version. `ReadHistory` and `Inspect` hide it and the table.
`running` and `failed` are "dirty". `rolled_back` is not dirty.

### How apply decides what to run

1. Take the migration lock, set session timeouts, create the history table if
   missing.
2. Refuse (`ErrDirty`, exit 3) if any row is `running` or `failed`.
3. Refuse (`ErrChecksumMismatch`, exit 3) on a checksum problem (above).
4. Pending = every `*.up.sql` and every registered Go migration (section 6a)
   whose version has no row other than
   `rolled_back`, run in ascending version order, optionally stopping after
   `--to N` (a version without a file is refused, so a typo applies nothing).

The test is "has no row", not "is newer than the latest applied". An older file
that appears later (a merged branch) is still applied, after newer ones.
`apply` does not check snapshot parents; `validate` does (section 2).

### Drift

`momo migrate drift` inspects the live database and compares it with the
snapshot of the **latest applied** migration. A database without momo history
(nothing applied, the case of [adopting a database](#7-adopting-an-existing-database))
is compared with the **latest snapshot in the migration directory** instead, the
schema `baseline` expects, so each differing object is named; a directory
without a snapshot compares with the empty schema, so every object is
unmanaged. Exit 0 and `no drift`, or exit 1 and one line per finding:

| Line                               | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `changed: <kind> <name>: <detail>` | In both, definition differs. A column, index or constraint present only live is `changed: ... not in snapshot` on that object. An invalid index is `changed: ... invalid index (failed CONCURRENTLY build)`.              |
| `missing: <kind> <name>`           | In the snapshot, not in the database.                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `unmanaged: <kind> <name>`         | In the database, not in the snapshot: tables, views, functions, enums, schemas, **extensions** (every extension except `plpgsql`, for example `pg_stat_statements`, `pgcrypto`), and triggers/policies on managed tables. |
| `unverified: <kind> <name>`        | Not compared and does not affect the exit code (below).                                                                                                                                                                   |

- A `changed:` line ends with `live: ...; snapshot: ...`: the fields that
  differ, with the value each side holds. For a column that lost its default and
  its NOT NULL: `live: default=none, nullable=true; snapshot: default="'new'", nullable=false`
  (`nullable=false` is NOT NULL). An object present only live lists its whole
  definition under `live:`.
- Extension versions are ignored when either side leaves the version empty.
- A sequence no column owns is a `sequence` object: `missing`, `unmanaged` or
  `changed` (the differing fields, such as `increment`) like any other.
- Hide objects you do not manage with `migrate.exclude` (globs over `name` or
  `schema.name`; they apply to tables, views, functions, enums, sequences,
  extensions, triggers and policies). Example: `exclude: ["pg_stat_statements", "audit_*"]`.
  PostgreSQL inspection applies the globs while it reads, before an object is
  examined: a matching table is skipped before its columns, constraints, indexes
  and partitions are read, a matching view or function before its definition is
  read, and a trigger whose own name or table matches before its definition is
  read. So an object the schema model cannot represent (for example a table with
  a `VIRTUAL` generated column) no longer fails `generate --from-db`, `baseline`
  or `drift` once you exclude it. Extensions, enums and policies are not skipped
  early; they are filtered afterwards as before. `generate --from-db` also
  passes every `introspect.skip` glob to inspection the same way, so a skipped
  table is never read (the globs also match views and functions of that name).
- A generated column is STORED unless `schema.Column.GeneratedVirtual` is set.
  MySQL inspection reads the kind from `EXTRA` and SQLite from `hidden` in
  `pragma_table_xinfo`, and both render `VIRTUAL` when it is set. A kind change
  is a diff change: SQLite rebuilds the table, and MySQL and PostgreSQL refuse
  it with "write a custom migration" because neither can switch the kind in
  place. A model declares the kind with the `virtual` tag option next to
  `generated:<expr>` (or `Config.GeneratedVirtual`). PostgreSQL has VIRTUAL
  columns only from version 18, which momo does not support yet: a `virtual`
  tag for a PostgreSQL target is a generate error, rendering one returns an
  error matching `momo.ErrUnsupported`, and PostgreSQL inspection still
  refuses a VIRTUAL column.

- An app that migrates in-process can load the same settings from an embedded
  `momo.yaml` with `migrate.ConfigFromFile(fsys, "momo.yaml")`; it returns the
  engine options the CLI builds from the `migrate:` section and `introspect.only`
  (see [upgrading](upgrading.md)).
- `migrate.Settings.OnlyTables` (set from `introspect.only` by the CLI) is the
  inverse for tables: when it is not empty, a table whose name or `schema.name`
  matches none of its globs is not managed. A table in the current schema is
  matched by its bare name only (its schema is empty), so write `users`, not
  `public.users`, when `public` is the current schema. Inspection does not read it
  (`migrate.InspectOptions.Only`, honoured by the PostgreSQL inspector), and
  drift, baseline and diff hide it, with its triggers and policies, like an
  excluded table. `migrate.MatchObject(globs, schemaName, name)` is the matching
  rule `Exclude`, `OnlyTables` and the inspector share. An empty entry is an
  error. `diff` filters both sides: a snapshot table outside `OnlyTables` never
  plans `DROP TABLE`, and a model for one never plans `CREATE TABLE`: a model
  for a table outside `only` is never migrated. Partition children are tables
  of their own: `only: [orders]` leaves out `orders_2024`; use
  `only: [orders, "orders_*"]`. The MySQL and SQLite inspectors ignore
  `InspectOptions.Only` and read every table; the filter is applied afterwards,
  so a table they cannot represent can still fail inspection.
- The PostgreSQL inspector skips an index that is attached to a parent
  partitioned index (a `pg_inherits` row on the index). Only the parent index
  is modeled; PostgreSQL creates, names and drops the partition indexes, so a
  fresh install has no duplicates and `drift` ignores partition index names
  that diverged after a column rename. Constraint-backed partition indexes were
  already skipped.
- A trigger limited to some columns (`AFTER UPDATE OF state`) is
  `schema.Trigger.UpdateOf`: PostgreSQL renders `UPDATE OF "state"`, inspection
  reads the list back and `generate --from-db` writes it into the model.
- `momo_migrations` is never reported.
- A view query, trigger `WHEN` and policy `USING`/`WITH CHECK` changed outside
  migrations is reported as `changed:` (the detail names `query`, `when`,
  `using` or `check`), and a body declared in another spelling than the server
  reports (`id>0` against `id > 0`) is not drift. To compare them, drift
  rewrites the snapshot's text through a scratch schema in a rolled-back
  transaction (the same step as `baseline`), which needs **`CREATE` on the
  database** and a writable session. No DDL runs against the application
  schema (`TestDriftBodiesRunsDDLOnlyInRolledBackTransaction`).
- A role that cannot do that (a read-only CI role, say) still gets a report:
  the bodies are listed as `unverified: <kind> <name>` and do not affect the
  exit code, so exit 0 does not prove they match. `momo migrate drift --strict`
  (`Engine.DriftWith(ctx, DriftOptions{Strict: true})`) turns that case into an
  error: exit 3 with a message wrapping `ErrCanonicalizePrivilege` that names
  the privilege. Use `--strict` where a clean report must mean the policies
  were checked, since a policy loosened to `USING (true)` hides in `unverified:`
  otherwise (`TestDriftBodiesNeedCreateOnDatabase`, both modes, as `momo_app`).
  Function bodies are compared in both modes.
- A snapshot without those bodies canonicalizes only its table text (defaults,
  checks, index predicates) through the same scratch schema. There drift stays
  tolerant: without `CREATE` it still runs and can show false `changed` entries
  (never hides a real one), and lists the tables it compared as declared in
  `CanonicalizeSkipped`.

### Repairing a database: `drift --fix-sql`

`momo migrate drift --fix-sql` prints the DDL that brings the live database to
the snapshot drift compares it with (the latest applied one, or, without
history, the latest snapshot in the directory). It is for a database another
tool built, so that adopting it needs no hand-written SQL: the refusal of
`baseline` names the differing objects, `drift --fix-sql` writes the fix.

- It only prints. The script goes to standard output, one statement per block,
  ended by a semicolon, in the order `diff` would write a migration (the
  statements that must run outside a transaction come last, behind a comment).
  Review it and run it yourself; momo applies nothing. Standard output is SQL
  only; everything else, including `no drift` for a clean database, goes to
  standard error. PostgreSQL runs the script in one transaction, and so does
  SQLite, except that a table rebuild needs `PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF` set
  outside the transaction (the script says so in a comment). MySQL and MariaDB
  do not roll DDL back: a step that fails (a constraint the data violates)
  leaves the steps before it applied, and standard error says so.
- It compares with the snapshot of the latest applied migration, or, without
  history, the latest snapshot in the directory. `--version N` compares with
  the snapshot of exactly version N instead, the one `baseline --version N`
  checks; use it when you adopt at the init version while the directory holds
  later migrations (`RepairOptions.Version` and `DriftOptions.Version` in Go).
  Standard error names the version that was compared
  (`DriftReport.SnapshotVersion`).
- It is rendered by the dialect's own differ and renderer, live to snapshot, so
  PostgreSQL, SQLite (a table rebuild where SQLite needs one) and MySQL/MariaDB
  each get their own SQL. A step the dialect cannot render is listed on standard
  error as `not rendered: ...`, never printed as wrong SQL, and the exit code is 1.
- Destructive steps are not printed: every drop (a table, column, index,
  constraint or view the snapshot does not have) and every column type change.
  Each is listed on standard error as `withheld: <change> <name>: <reason>`,
  together with the steps that depend on it and the creates that would replace
  it (a changed view, trigger, policy, index or constraint is a drop and a
  create of the same name, and printing the create alone would fail with
  `already exists`), and the exit code is 1. Pass
  `--allow-destructive` to print them too. On SQLite, a step that needs a table
  rebuild is withheld while another step of the same table is, because the
  rebuild would apply it.
- A NOT NULL column that is missing is added nullable (the table may hold rows).
  Standard error lists it as `staged: ...` with the `ALTER TABLE ... SET NOT NULL`
