This page says what Momo promises to keep working once it is at version 1,
what it does not promise, how a deprecated API is retired, and how that
differs from the pre-v1 releases you can install today. The promise only
starts at v1; until then read [how pre-v1 differs](#how-pre-v1-differs-today).

## What the promise covers

From v1, a minor or patch release does not break a program or a
repository that worked with an earlier `1.x` release. The promise covers these
surfaces:

| Surface                  | What stays compatible                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Exported Go API          | every exported identifier of the covered packages: names, signatures, types, struct fields, interface method sets, constants and the documented behavior, including the sentinel errors that `errors.Is` matches                         |
| Generated code shape     | code that `momo generate` wrote with any `1.x` release compiles and behaves with every later `1.y` runtime; this is why the descriptor constructors that look internal, such as `momo.NewColumn`, are covered                            |
| CLI flags and exit codes | the commands, flags and flag values in `momo help`, the exit codes 0, 1, 2 and 3 and what each means, and the text `momo generate --check` uses for a stale file; the wording of diagnostics and of human-readable output is not covered |
| `momo.yaml` keys         | a key that `gen/config` reads keeps its name, type and meaning; a new key is optional and has a default that keeps the old behavior; `version: 1` keeps loading                                                                          |
| Snapshot, history, sum   | `schema.FormatVersion`, `migrate.SnapshotFormat`, `migrate.SumFormat` and `migrate.HistoryFormat` (the history table) keep reading what an earlier `1.x` wrote; a release may add optional fields but never changes the meaning of one   |
| Model declarations       | the `momo` struct tag grammar and option names, the `momo.Model`, `momo.View` and `momo.Projection` markers and the `MomoConfig` method: an option keeps its meaning and a new one is an addition                                        |
| Generator plugin API     | `gen.PluginAPIVersion` stays at 1 for the whole `1.x` line; a plugin built for it keeps running                                                                                                                                          |

Compatible means source compatible for the exported Go API, as `apidiff`
(`golang.org/x/exp/cmd/apidiff`) judges it: adding an identifier, a method to a
struct or a field to a struct is compatible; adding a method to an exported
interface that users implement, removing or renaming anything, or changing a
signature is not. The `apidiff-docs` CI job checks this on every pull request
(see [the gate](#how-the-gate-enforces-it)).

A newer snapshot, history table or `momo.sum` than a binary understands is
refused with `schema.ErrNewerFormat` rather than read wrongly; the reverse,
an older file read by a newer binary, always works.

Behavior bug fixes are not breaking changes. A fix that makes Momo refuse
what it used to accept wrongly (an invalid identifier, a wrong dialect
statement) is a fix, and the changelog says so. A security fix may break
compatibility in a minor release when there is no other way; the release notes
and [upgrading](upgrading.md) say how to adapt.

## What is excluded

These are outside the promise. They can change in any release.

| Excluded                                                                         | Why                                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `gen/graphql`, `gen/grpc`, `gen/openapi`                                         | ecosystem generators and their runtime helpers follow gqlgen, protobuf and OpenAPI tooling that Momo does not control |
| `gen/apiquery`                                                                   | the helper surface of the generated API handlers, tied to the generators above                                        |
| `importer` and `importer/...`                                                    | readers of other ORMs' models and migration history; they track those tools' formats                                  |
| `internal/...`                                                                   | not importable; includes `internal/testdb`, `internal/suite` and the other test support                               |
| `momotest`, `momotest/sqlitetest`, `migrate/migratetest`                         | test helpers: their assertions, fixtures and defaults may change to catch more mistakes                               |
| `bench` and `examples/...`                                                       | separate benchmark module and runnable examples                                                                       |
| the `otelmomo` module                                                            | versioned and tagged on its own (`otelmomo/vX.Y.Z`), so it carries its own promise from its own v1                    |
| the exact SQL text, the wording of errors and diagnostics, the layout of reports | the sentinel errors and error types are covered; the SQL Momo writes and the messages it prints are not               |
| anything marked experimental in its doc comment                                  | not covered by the promise, but the gate does not read doc comments: list the package or declare the change breaking  |

The `apidiff-docs` gate knows the excluded packages from
`scripts/apidiff-experimental.txt`, read from the merge base so that a pull
request cannot exempt its own change. The file lists the `gen/graphql`,
`gen/grpc`, `gen/openapi`, `gen/apiquery` and `importer` rows above. The other
rows are outside the gate already (`internal`, nested modules) or are not API
(the SQL text, messages). The gate does not filter by doc comment: a pull
request that changes an identifier marked experimental in a covered package
must be declared breaking, or the package must be listed first. Adding a
package to the covered set later is a compatible change; moving a covered
package to the excluded set is not allowed within `1.x`.

## Interfaces and dependencies with their own rules

- `migrate.Dialect` and the optional interfaces a migration dialect may
  implement are implemented only by Momo's `migrate/postgres`,
  `migrate/sqlite` and `migrate/mysql`. A `1.x` release may add a method to
  them; code outside Momo calls a dialect but does not implement one.
- `driver/pgxdriver` is the pgx v5 adapter, and pgx types appear in its
  signatures (`pgxdriver.New` takes a `*pgxpool.Pool`). It follows pgx v5 for
  the whole `1.x` line; a later pgx major version gets a new driver package
  instead of a change to this one. `pgxdriver.PgxTx` and
  `pgxdriver.UnwrapPgxTx` are the supported way to move between a pgx
  transaction and a `momo.Tx`.
- The gate runs `apidiff` under one build configuration, so identifiers that
  exist only in a cgo build, such as those of `driver/sqlitedriver`, are not
  compared by it. A change to them is reviewed by hand.

## The expression extension API

Code outside Momo may define its own typed expressions, and the surface for
that is deliberately small. These names are the extension API, covered like any
other exported identifier, and nothing else in the root package is an
extension point:

| Name                          | Why a minimal external expression needs it                                                                                                                                  |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `momo.Expr`                   | the one method, `AppendSQL`, that every fragment implements                                                                                                                 |
| `momo.Expression`             | the typed form: an `Expression[bool]` is a `momo.Predicate`, so the compiler checks operand types                                                                           |
| `momo.Ops`                    | embedding `momo.Ops[T]` gives the host the comparison and ordering methods (`Eq`, `In`, `Between`, `Asc` and the rest) without writing them                                 |
| `momo.NewOps`                 | binds the embedded `momo.Ops` to the finished host; there is no other way to build one                                                                                      |
| `momo.Typed`                  | gives a plain `momo.Expr` a result type, for a fragment that needs no comparison methods of its own                                                                         |
| `momo.Flagged`                | lets a wrapper forward the flags of the column it wraps, so a value compared with a sensitive column stays masked in hook events through the wrapper                        |
| `momo.ColumnFlags`            | the result type of `momo.Flagged`                                                                                                                                           |
| `(*momo.Builder).Ident`       | writes a quoted identifier; names never go into the SQL as text                                                                                                             |
| `(*momo.Builder).Arg`         | binds a value as a parameter; values never go into the SQL as text                                                                                                          |
| `(*momo.Builder).Dialect`     | lets the expression choose its SQL or refuse a dialect                                                                                                                      |
| `(*momo.Builder).SetErr`      | reports a bad argument or an unsupported dialect, with a `*momo.Error` of kind `momo.ErrValidation` or `momo.ErrUnsupported`                                                |
| `(*momo.Builder).WriteString` | writes the fixed SQL text of the expression (keywords, operators, punctuation); without it an expression could only write identifiers and parameters, never a function call |

The example attached to `momo.NewOps` in the root package's tests is a worked
expression built from these names alone, and CI compiles and runs it.

Everything else that agg, arrayop, fts, jsonop, rangeop, sqlfn, timeop and
vecop needed (binding a value with the sensitive-column mask, rendering an
operand to learn whether it read a sensitive column, a FILTER clause, a
bound-value check, name validation and a window wrapper) is behind an internal
bridge that only the packages of this module can import. Those names are not
promised, and a limit follows from that: a value that a custom expression binds
with `Builder.Arg` itself is not masked when the expression compares with a
sensitive column, so compare through the `momo.Ops` methods when an operand can
be one. The names that left the extension API stay as deprecated forwarders for one
release; [upgrading](upgrading.md) lists them.

### Generated-code support

`momo.NewColumn`, `momo.NewNullColumn`, `momo.NewReadOnlyColumn`,
`momo.NewNullReadOnlyColumn`, `momo.NewCreateOnlyColumn`,
`momo.NewImmutableColumn` and the six `momo.NewVectorColumn` variants exist for
the code `momo generate` writes. Their flags parameter is a `momo.ColumnFlags`,
built from the `momo.Flag*` constants, and `momo.ColumnMeta.Flags` has the same
type. They are covered by the generated code shape promise above, so they stay
stable even though application code should use the generated column variables
instead of calling them.

## Deprecation

An API leaves in two steps: it is deprecated, and much later it is removed.

1. A deprecated identifier, flag or `momo.yaml` key gets a `Deprecated:`
   paragraph in its doc comment that names the replacement
   (`// Deprecated: use X instead.`). Tools such as staticcheck report uses of it.
   The replacement exists in the same release, so a user can move at once.
2. The release notes (`CHANGELOG.md`) and [upgrading](upgrading.md) list it
   with a rewrite recipe. A deprecated CLI flag or `momo.yaml` key keeps working
   and prints a warning to standard error.
3. A deprecated identifier stays for at least one full minor release after the
   one that announced it. In the covered surface it is then removed only in the
   next major version, because removing it earlier is an incompatible change.
   In an excluded package it may be removed from the second minor release after
   the announcement.
4. A deprecated identifier keeps its documented behavior and keeps its tests.
   It receives security fixes, but not new features.

## How the gate enforces it

The `apidiff-docs` job runs `make apidiff-gate` on every pull request
(`scripts/apidiff-docs-gate.sh`). It compares the exported API of every
non-internal package in the root module between the base branch and the pull
request.

- Before v1 the gate only demands a docs change for an exported change, as
  [contributing](contributing.md) describes. It never fails an incompatible
  change on its own.
- From v1 it also fails an incompatible change in a covered package unless
  the pull request is declared breaking: the title has a `!` after the type
  (`feat!: remove X`; the type is matched in any case), or the pull request
  body or a commit message has a line that starts in column 0 with
  `BREAKING CHANGE: ` or `BREAKING-CHANGE: ` and a description. A declared
  breaking change ships in the next major version; release-please reads the
  same markers to choose it.
- A major version above 1 also needs a new module path,
  `github.com/azrtydxb/momo/v2`. release-please does not change the module
  path, `go.mod` or the import paths, so that release is a manual step the
  maintainer takes then; the gate does not check it.

The gate reads the module version from `.release-please-manifest.json` and the
excluded packages from `scripts/apidiff-experimental.txt`, both on the merge
base, so a pull request cannot switch the gate off or exempt its own change by
editing either file. It reads the manifest only when a covered package has an
incompatible change, and a manifest it cannot read counts as pre-v1. The exact
rule is in the header of `scripts/apidiff-docs-gate.sh`; the filter that drops
the excluded packages is `scripts/apidiff-incompatible.sh`, and
`internal/repocheck` tests it against apidiff-shaped output.

## How pre-v1 differs today

Momo is pre-v1. None of the promises above applies to the releases you can
install now, and this is what holds instead:

- A `0.y` minor release may break the exported API, the generated code, a CLI
  flag, a `momo.yaml` key or a file format. release-please runs with
  `bump-minor-pre-major`, so a breaking change raises the minor number, and the
  commit is marked `feat!:` or has a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.
- There is no deprecation window. An identifier can be removed in the release
  after the one that deprecated it, or in the same release when no replacement
  is needed.
- The `apidiff-docs` gate does not fail an incompatible change; it asks for a
  docs change only.
- Snapshot, history and sum files carry the format versions above and a newer
  one is refused, but a `0.y` release can still raise a version; read
  [upgrading](upgrading.md) before each upgrade.
- Pin an exact version in `go.mod`, read `CHANGELOG.md` before you upgrade and
  run `momo generate` again afterwards; [supported versions](supported-versions.md)
  keeps the stability table.

Which packages are excluded and the deprecation rules are written down now so
that a review of the exported API before v1 can change what needs to
change; they take effect when the version tag does.


# Source: upgrading.md

# Upgrading

Momo is pre-v1 and makes no compatibility promise between releases; see the
[stability policy](supported-versions.md#stability-policy). Read this page and
the `CHANGELOG.md` entry of a release before you upgrade, and expect that
later releases can break more.

## Upgrading to 0.20.0

Every driver package now has the same two constructors, so code that opens a
SQLite or MySQL database must change: `sqlitedriver.Open`, `sqlitepure.Open`,
`mysqldriver.Open` and `mysqldriver.New` take different arguments and no longer
return a `*sql.DB`. Six option and helper names also changed so that every
functional option is spelled With plus what it sets, the 20 advisory lock
functions became two functions with options, the statement N+1 detector moved
into `obs` and now shares one scope with the relation-load detector, and the
hook constructors return their concrete types. Names that two packages shared or
that broke a naming rule were renamed too: `migrate.Config` and `gen.Config`,
`migrate.FormatVersion`, the date functions of `sqlfn`, the PostgreSQL names of
`fts`, a few `sqlfn` and `timeop` pairs, and the `momotest` seed steps (the
table is in the section on colliding names below). The old `pgxdriver` names, the
renamed options, the advisory functions, the old N+1 names and the old names of
that table stay as deprecated aliases or forwarders for this release and run the
same statements, so that code keeps compiling and behaving as before; move to
the new names before the forwarders go. Beyond the driver constructors, the
changes that can stop code compiling are a hook constructor result that you
assert to an interface or assign to a variable of another type, and
`sqlitetest.New`, which now takes the options of `momotest`, and code outside
this module that defines its own typed expressions or passes a bare `uint16` as
column flags (the last section of this page). Separately,
`momo migrate drift`, `momo migrate baseline` and `momo generate --from-db` now
see exclusion constraints on PostgreSQL and write range columns as `types.Range`
fields (the first two sections below); no edit is needed in your code for that,
but inspection of a database that holds an exclusion constraint momo cannot
model now stops with an error.

### Exclusion constraints are part of the schema

Before, inspection skipped the constraints of kind `x` in `pg_constraint`, so a
database with `EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)` read as a
table without it, and the init migration that `generate --from-db` produced
built the table without the rule. Inspection now reads each one, and `momo
generate --from-db` writes it as a `Config.Exclude` declaration. A snapshot you
already have loads with no exclusion constraints, so the snapshot format version
is unchanged and no snapshot needs rewriting.

If your database has one, `drift` and `baseline` now report it as missing from
the snapshot until the snapshot says so. Run `momo generate --from-db` again, or
declare it in `MomoConfig` and run `momo migrate diff`. A constraint with a
`WHERE` predicate, an expression, an operator class or an ordering is not
modelled: inspection stops with an error that names it and its table. Hide the
table with `migrate.exclude`, and keep the constraint in a migration written by
hand. See [migrations](migrations.md#exclusion-constraints).

### Range columns map to `types.Range`

`generate --from-db` mapped no range type before, so a table with an `int4range`
or `tstzrange` column stopped the generation until an `introspect` types rule
named a Go type for it. The six built-in range types now map to
`types.Range[T]`: `int4range` to `types.Range[int32]`, `int8range` to
`types.Range[int64]`, `numrange` to `types.Range[types.Numeric]`, `daterange` to
`types.Range[types.Date]`, `tsrange` to `types.Range[types.Timestamp]` and
`tstzrange` to `types.Range[time.Time]`. A rule you wrote for such a column still
wins. See [type mapping](TYPE_MAPPING.md#range-types).

### One constructor shape for every driver

`New(handle, opts...)` wraps a pool or `*sql.DB` you opened, does not own it and
never closes it. `Open(ctx, dsn, opts...)` opens the database, owns it and
returns `(momo.Driver, error)`; the new `momo.DB.Close` closes the pool it
opened, and does nothing to a pool you passed to `New`. Before, nothing said
who closed what: the
SQLite and MySQL `Open` returned the `*sql.DB` for you to close, and
`pgxdriver.NewPool` returned a pool.

| Before                                                               | After                                                                                                                        |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `db, drv, err := sqlitedriver.Open(dsn, cfg)`                        | `drv, err := sqlitedriver.Open(ctx, dsn, sqlitedriver.WithConfig(cfg))`                                                      |
| `db, drv, err := sqlitepure.Open(dsn, cfg)`                          | `drv, err := sqlitepure.Open(ctx, dsn, sqlitepure.WithConfig(cfg))`                                                          |
| `sqlitepure.Config{ReadOnly: true}`                                  | `sqlitepure.WithReadOnly()`                                                                                                  |
| `db, drv, err := mysqldriver.Open(dsn, dialect.FlavorMariaDB)`       | `drv, err := mysqldriver.Open(ctx, dsn, mysqldriver.WithFlavor(dialect.FlavorMariaDB))`                                      |
| `mysqldriver.New(db, dialect.FlavorMariaDB)`                         | `mysqldriver.New(db, mysqldriver.WithFlavor(dialect.FlavorMariaDB))`                                                         |
| `pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, url)` and `pgxdriver.New(pool)` | `drv, err := pgxdriver.Open(ctx, url)`; `NewPool` and `New` stay for a program that needs the pool                           |
| `pgxdriver.FromSQLDB(db)`                                            | `pgxdriver.NewSQL(db)` (`FromSQLDB` is deprecated)                                                                           |
| `db, drv := pgxdriver.FromConnConfig(cfg)`                           | `drv, err := pgxdriver.OpenSQL(ctx, dsn)`, or `stdlib.OpenDB(*cfg)` with `pgxdriver.NewSQL` (`FromConnConfig` is deprecated) |
| `sqlitedriver.SQLiteVecVersion`                                      | `sqlitedriver.VecVersion` (`SQLiteVecVersion` is deprecated)                                                                 |

Close an opened driver with `db.Close()`: after
`drv, err := sqlitepure.Open(ctx, "app.db")` and `db := momo.New(drv)`, call it
once, for example in a `defer`, when you are done with `db` and with every
transaction begun from it. A second call is safe.

`pgxdriver.Open` and `pgxdriver.OpenSQL` now ping the server on `ctx`, so an
unreachable server or a bad password is an error at `Open`, as it already was
for SQLite and MySQL; `pgxdriver.NewPool` still does not dial. `New` refuses an
option that tries to configure a pool that is already open: the SQLite `New`
with `WithBusyTimeout` or another setting, and `pgxdriver.NewSQL` with
`WithExecMode` or `WithVectorFormat`, return a driver whose every call fails
with `ErrValidation` naming the option. Set those on your own `*sql.DB` or
`*pgx.ConnConfig` instead; `pgxdriver.OpenSQL` takes `WithExecMode` itself.

If you need the `*sql.DB` itself, for your own queries or to share it, open it
yourself and wrap it: `sqlitepure.New(sqlDB)` does not own it, so you close it.
A MariaDB server needs `mysqldriver.WithFlavor(dialect.FlavorMariaDB)`; the
default flavor is MySQL.

### Settings are options and the types are public

`sqlitedriver.Config` and `sqlitepure.Config` are now declared in their own
packages instead of aliasing one internal type. They have the same fields, so
`sqlitepure.Config(cfg)` converts one to the other; they are no longer
identical types. `gen/config.MigrateConfig` is declared in `gen/config` too.
`sqlitedriver.SQLiteVecVersion` is renamed `VecVersion`: one name in both
builds, a constant that is `"v0.1.6"` with cgo and `""` without, because
sqlite-vec is not linked then. A build without cgo, or for Windows, has the same
`Open`, `New` and option names as the cgo build, so code compiles either way;
`Open` returns `ErrUnsupported` there and `New` returns a driver whose every
call does.

### One N+1 detector family and one scope

Before, `momo.NewNPlusOneHook` counted statement shapes in a scope made with
`momo.WithQueryScope`, and `obs.NewNPlusOne` counted relation loads in a scope
made with `obs.WithScope`. A request that wanted both detectors had to be
wrapped twice, and the two names did not say which counted what. Both detectors
now live in `obs` and read the one scope that `obs.WithScope` makes, so you wrap
the context once and register one or both. They keep separate counts inside it.

| Before                                               | After                                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `momo.NewNPlusOneHook(n, report)`                    | `obs.NewStatementNPlusOne(n, report)`                       |
| `momo.NPlusOneFinding` (`Shape`, `Example`, `Count`) | `obs.StatementFinding` (the same three fields)              |
| `momo.WithQueryScope(ctx)`                           | `obs.WithScope(ctx)`                                        |
| `obs.NewNPlusOne(n, report)` with `obs.WithScope`    | unchanged; the scope now also serves the statement detector |

Replace the three `momo` names with the `obs` ones. The `momo` names are marked
`Deprecated:` and are removed in the release after this one. They count exactly
as the `obs` detector does, and `momo.WithQueryScope` returns the scope
`obs.WithScope` makes, so you can move one call site at a time: a context made
by either serves the detectors of both. The finding type is a separate type with
the same fields, so a `report` function that takes `momo.NPlusOneFinding` takes
`obs.StatementFinding` after the move.

Two behaviors changed with the shared scope. A context made by `obs.WithScope`
now also drives the deprecated `momo.NewNPlusOneHook`. Nesting `obs.WithScope`
inside `momo.WithQueryScope`, or the reverse, now replaces the outer scope and
restarts the counts, so wrap the context once per unit of work.

### Hook constructors return their concrete types

Before, `obs.NewNPlusOne` returned `*obs.NPlusOne` while `obs.NewSlowQuery` and
`momolog.New` returned `momo.Hook` and `otelmomo.New` returned
`(momo.Hook, error)`. Each constructor now returns the type it builds, which
still implements `momo.Hook`, so `momo.WithHook(h)` is unchanged.

| Constructor                | Before               | After                     |
| -------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `obs.NewSlowQuery`         | `momo.Hook`          | `*obs.SlowQueryHook`      |
| `momolog.New`              | `momo.Hook`          | `*momolog.Hook`           |
| `otelmomo.New`             | `(momo.Hook, error)` | `(*otelmomo.Hook, error)` |
| `obs.NewStatementNPlusOne` | new                  | `*obs.StatementNPlusOne`  |

Code that passes the result to `momo.WithHook` needs no edit. Code that stores
it in a variable of type `momo.Hook` still compiles. Code that type-asserts the
result, as in `momolog.New(l).(momo.RelationHook)`, no longer compiles because
the result is not an interface; assign it to a `momo.Hook` first, or call the
methods on the concrete type. A variable that you declared with `:=` and later
assigned a different hook to now has a concrete type and rejects that
assignment; declare it as `momo.Hook`. `otelmomo` is a separate module with its
own release, so this change reaches it in its own next release; `momo.NewNPlusOneHook`
keeps returning `momo.Hook` because it is a deprecated forwarder.

### Functional options are named `With*`

| Old name                     | New name                    |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `momolog.Level`              | `momolog.WithLevel`         |
| `momolog.SlowOver`           | `momolog.WithSlowThreshold` |
| `momolog.Values`             | `momolog.WithValues`        |
| `advisory.Hash64`            | `advisory.WithHash64`       |
| `pgxdriver.OnReconnect`      | `pgxdriver.WithOnReconnect` |
| `momo.WithDetail` (an error) | `momo.Annotate`             |

`momo.WithDetail` is not an option: it copies an error with its raw driver
detail set, so it is now `momo.Annotate`. The With prefix is kept for options
and for context wrappers such as `momo.WithTenant`, which keep the shape of
`context.WithValue`; the rule is in the package comment of `momo` and in the
contributor guide. The arguments and the behavior of every renamed function are
unchanged, so `gofmt -r` renames a call site:

```sh
gofmt -r 'momolog.Level -> momolog.WithLevel' -w .
gofmt -r 'momolog.SlowOver -> momolog.WithSlowThreshold' -w .
gofmt -r 'momolog.Values -> momolog.WithValues' -w .
gofmt -r 'advisory.Hash64 -> advisory.WithHash64' -w .
gofmt -r 'pgxdriver.OnReconnect -> pgxdriver.WithOnReconnect' -w .
gofmt -r 'momo.WithDetail -> momo.Annotate' -w .
```

### Advisory locks are `advisory.Acquire` and `advisory.Release`

`advisory.Acquire(ctx, q, key, opts...)` takes a lock and returns whether it is
held; `advisory.Release(ctx, q, key, opts...)` releases a session lock. The key
is an `int64` (or `int`) or a string, so the `...String` forms are gone, and
three options choose the lock: `advisory.Xact` (transaction-scoped, `q` is the
`*momo.Tx`), `advisory.Shared` and `advisory.Try` (return `false` instead of
waiting). `advisory.Acquire` without `advisory.Try` blocks and returns `true`.
A session lock still needs the pinned `*momo.DB` of `db.OnConn(pc)`. The old
functions map like this, with `K` an `int64` or a string key:

| Old call                                 | New call                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `advisory.XactLock(ctx, tx, K)`          | `advisory.Acquire(ctx, tx, K, advisory.Xact())`                                    |
| `advisory.TryXactLock(ctx, tx, K)`       | `advisory.Acquire(ctx, tx, K, advisory.Xact(), advisory.Try())`                    |
| `advisory.XactLockShared(ctx, tx, K)`    | `advisory.Acquire(ctx, tx, K, advisory.Xact(), advisory.Shared())`                 |
| `advisory.TryXactLockShared(ctx, tx, K)` | `advisory.Acquire(ctx, tx, K, advisory.Xact(), advisory.Shared(), advisory.Try())` |
| `advisory.Lock(ctx, db, K)`              | `advisory.Acquire(ctx, db, K)`                                                     |
| `advisory.TryLock(ctx, db, K)`           | `advisory.Acquire(ctx, db, K, advisory.Try())`                                     |
| `advisory.Unlock(ctx, db, K)`            | `advisory.Release(ctx, db, K)`                                                     |
| `advisory.LockShared(ctx, db, K)`        | `advisory.Acquire(ctx, db, K, advisory.Shared())`                                  |
| `advisory.TryLockShared(ctx, db, K)`     | `advisory.Acquire(ctx, db, K, advisory.Shared(), advisory.Try())`                  |
| `advisory.UnlockShared(ctx, db, K)`      | `advisory.Release(ctx, db, K, advisory.Shared())`                                  |

The `...String` forms (`advisory.XactLockString`, `advisory.LockString`,
`advisory.UnlockSharedString` and the other seven) map the same way with a
string key, and keep taking the hash option, now `advisory.WithHash64`; they
refuse any other option with `ErrValidation`. Two differences to know:

- `advisory.Acquire` and `advisory.Release` take a `momo.Querier`, so a
  `*momo.DB` with `advisory.Xact` and a `*momo.Tx` without it fail at run time
  with `ErrValidation` where the old transaction functions failed to compile.
- `advisory.Acquire` returns `(bool, error)` for the blocking form too, so
  assign or discard the boolean.

### Colliding and inconsistent names are renamed

Before, `momo.Config` (the model marker), `migrate.Config` and `gen.Config` were
three unrelated types with one name, `sqlfn.DateExpr` and `timeop.DateExpr`
were two different types, `momo.Rank` (a window function) and `fts.Rank`
(`ts_rank`) shared a word, and a few function pairs did not follow the rule that
`X` takes Go values and `XExpr` takes expressions. Each old name below is kept
for this release as a deprecated alias or forwarder that runs the same code,
except `sqlitetest.New`, which has one signature and cannot keep two.

| Old name                                        | New name                                                         |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `migrate.Config`                                | `migrate.Settings`                                               |
| `migrate.WithConfig`                            | `migrate.WithSettings`                                           |
| `gen.Config`                                    | `gen.LoadConfig`                                                 |
| `migrate.FormatVersion` (the history table)     | `migrate.HistoryFormat`                                          |
| `sqlfn.CurrentDate`                             | `timeop.CurrentDate`                                             |
| `sqlfn.Infinity`, `sqlfn.NegInfinity`           | `timeop.Infinity`, `timeop.NegInfinity`                          |
| `sqlfn.DateExpr`                                | `timeop.Expr`                                                    |
| `fts.ToVector`                                  | `fts.TSVector`                                                   |
| `fts.ToQuery`                                   | `fts.TSQuery`                                                    |
| `fts.WebsearchToQuery`                          | `fts.TSWebsearchQuery`                                           |
| `fts.PlainToQuery`                              | `fts.TSPlainQuery`                                               |
| `fts.PhraseToQuery`                             | `fts.TSPhraseQuery`                                              |
| `fts.Match`                                     | `fts.TSMatch`                                                    |
| `fts.Rank`                                      | `fts.TSRank`                                                     |
| `fts.RankCD`                                    | `fts.TSRankCD`                                                   |
| `fts.Headline`                                  | `fts.TSHeadline`                                                 |
| `sqlfn.SubstrFrom`                              | `sqlfn.SubstrToEnd`; `sqlfn.SubstrExpr` is new                   |
| `timeop.IntervalExpr`                           | `timeop.IntervalOfExpr`                                          |
| `momotest.Insert`                               | `momotest.Rows`                                                  |
| `momotest.Graph`                                | `momotest.GraphOf`                                               |
| `sqlitetest.New(tb, momo.WithHook(h))`          | `sqlitetest.New(tb, momotest.WithMomoOptions(momo.WithHook(h)))` |
| `sqlitetest.Template.New(tb, momo.WithHook(h))` | `tpl.New(tb, momotest.WithMomoOptions(momo.WithHook(h)))`        |

Notes on the rows that are more than a rename:

- `sqlfn.NullIf` now takes `T any`, the constraint `sqlfn.NullIfExpr` always had,
  so `sqlfn.NullIf(name, "")` compiles. Every call that compiled before renders
  the same SQL.
- `momo.Coalesce` takes a bound fallback and `sqlfn.CoalesceExpr` takes
  expressions, the value and expression forms of one function; both stay.
  `momo.Func` calls any scalar function and `agg.Func` calls an aggregate.
- `sqlitetest.New` and `momotest.New` take the same `momotest.Option`.
  `sqlitetest` honors `momotest.WithMomoOptions` and ignores the options that
  configure a PostgreSQL server (`momotest.WithEnv`, `momotest.WithMigrations`,
  `momotest.WithExtensions`, `momotest.WithMaxConns`, `momotest.WithTemplateClone`).
- `momo.Model`, `momo.View`, `momo.Projection` and `momo.Config` keep their
  names: they are the markers that models embed and that `MomoConfig` receives,
  and the collision was with the two engine types renamed above.
- `schema.FormatVersion` and `gen.FormatVersion` keep their names; they version
  the snapshot and the generated-file formats, and `migrate.HistoryFormat`
  versions the history table.

The nine raw SQL functions follow one rule: a function that runs hand-written
SQL is a verb and a function that wraps it for a builder ends in `SQL`, and no
name carries the word Raw. `momo.Exec`, `momo.Query`, `momo.QueryRows`,
`momo.SQL` and `momo.TypedSQL` already followed it and keep their names. The
other four are renamed, with identical signatures; the old names are deprecated
forwarders for this release:

| Old name           | New name             |
| ------------------ | -------------------- |
| `momo.Scalars`     | `momo.QueryScalars`  |
| `momo.RawRows`     | `momo.QueryCursor`   |
| `momo.RawSubquery` | `momo.SubquerySQL`   |
| `momo.RawQuery`    | `momo.CompilableSQL` |

`momovet` checks the new names and the deprecated ones alike.

### The expression extension API is small, and column flags have a type

Code outside this module may define its own typed expressions, and the surface
for that is now frozen and small: `momo.Expr`, `momo.Expression`, `momo.Ops`,
`momo.NewOps`, `momo.Typed` and `momo.Flagged`, and on `*momo.Builder` the
methods `Ident`, `Arg`, `momo.Builder.Dialect`, `SetErr` and `WriteString`. The other names
that the docs called extension points moved behind an internal bridge that only
the packages of this module (`agg`, `arrayop`, `fts`, `jsonop`, `rangeop`,
`sqlfn`, `timeop` and `vecop`) can import. They stay as deprecated forwarders
with their old signatures for this release, so existing code keeps compiling;
move off them before the next release, which removes them.

| Old name                                  | What to do                                                                                                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `momo.NewBuilder`                         | render through a query: `momo.NewOffline(dialect.Postgres)` and the `SQL` method of a query builder                                                   |
| `(*momo.Builder).WriteByte`               | `WriteString` with the one-character string                                                                                                           |
| `(*momo.Builder).ArgFor`                  | `Arg`, and compare through the `momo.Ops` methods, which mask a value compared with a sensitive column                                                |
| `(*momo.Builder).RenderSensitive`         | no replacement; `momo.Ops` comparisons do this for the host                                                                                           |
| `(*momo.Builder).ExprFor`                 | no replacement; `momo.Ops` comparisons do this for the host                                                                                           |
| `(*momo.Builder).MarkSensitive`           | no replacement; a column reference records itself when it renders                                                                                     |
| `(*momo.Builder).AppendFilter`            | no replacement outside the module; `agg.Call.Filter` and `momo.FilteredAgg` write the clause                                                          |
| `(*momo.Builder).Unsupported`             | `SetErr` with a `*momo.Error` carrying a kind `momo.ErrUnsupported`                                                                                   |
| `momo.FlagsOf`                            | assert `momo.Flagged` on the expression                                                                                                               |
| `momo.IsBound`                            | no replacement                                                                                                                                        |
| `momo.PredicateFunc`                      | a type that embeds `momo.Ops[bool]`, or `momo.Typed[bool]` around an `momo.Expr`                                                                      |
| `momo.ValidName` and `momo.ValidTypeName` | no replacement; validate the name in your own code                                                                                                    |
| `momo.WindowOf`                           | no replacement; `agg.Call.Over` builds the window function of an aggregate, and its result is now `agg.WindowExpr[T]` instead of `momo.WindowExpr[T]` |
| `momo.VectorColumnOf`                     | call `Table`, `ColumnName`, `Dim` and `Flags` on the vector column itself                                                                             |
| `momo.MetaTableSchema`                    | read `TableSchema` from the model's `MomoMeta()`                                                                                                      |
| `momo.Order.AppendOrder`                  | no replacement outside the module; `agg.Call.OrderBy` renders the ORDER BY of an ordered aggregate                                                    |

Two changes cannot keep their old shape. `agg.Call.Over` returns an
`agg.WindowExpr[T]`, a type of its own with `As` and the `momo.Ops` methods, so
a variable declared as `momo.WindowExpr[T]` that you assign it to must change to
the `agg` type or to `momo.Expression[T]`. And the column flags are a named
type: `momo.ColumnFlags` replaces `uint16` in `momo.ColumnMeta.Flags`, in the
`momo.NewColumn` family of constructors, in `momo.Flagged` and in the
`momo.Flag*` constants. Generated code and any call that passes the constants or
an untyped number compiles unchanged, so run `momo generate` only if you want
to; a variable or parameter of type `uint16` that holds flags must become
`momo.ColumnFlags`. A type that implements `Flags() uint16` no longer satisfies
`momo.Flagged`, but for this release `momo.Ops` and keyset pagination still
read its flags, so a sensitive column it wraps stays masked. Change its result
type to `momo.ColumnFlags` before the next release, which drops that path.

The `momo.NewColumn` family (`NewNullColumn`, `NewReadOnlyColumn`,
`NewNullReadOnlyColumn`, `NewCreateOnlyColumn`, `NewImmutableColumn` and the six
`NewVectorColumn` variants) is generated-code support: it is called by what
`momo generate` writes and kept stable for that code, and hand-written code
should use the generated column variables. [The compatibility
policy](compatibility.md#the-expression-extension-api) lists the frozen surface
and the reason for each name in it.

## Upgrading to 0.19.0

`momo migrate drift`, the refusal of `momo migrate baseline` and
`momo generate --from-db` now see `DEFERRABLE` constraints on PostgreSQL; no
edit is needed in your code, but a database that holds a deferrable constraint
your snapshot does not describe now reports a difference.

### Deferrable constraints are part of the schema

Before, momo ignored `DEFERRABLE` and `INITIALLY DEFERRED` on unique, primary
key and foreign key constraints: inspection did not read them, `generate
--from-db` wrote a plain constraint and the init migration it produced built
one, so a transaction that relied on a deferred check failed on a fresh install
with a unique violation. Inspection now reads `pg_constraint.condeferrable`
and `condeferred`, and `momo generate --from-db` writes them as
`IndexOpts.Deferrable`, `IndexOpts.InitiallyDeferred`,
`ForeignKeyOpts.Deferrable`, `ForeignKeyOpts.InitiallyDeferred`,
`Config.PrimaryKeyDeferrable` and `Config.PrimaryKeyInitiallyDeferred`
declarations. A snapshot you already have loads as not deferrable, so the
snapshot format version is unchanged and no snapshot needs rewriting.

If your database has such a constraint, `drift` and `baseline` now report it as
changed until the snapshot says so. Run `momo generate --from-db` again, or
declare the constraint in `MomoConfig` and run `momo migrate diff`, which drops
and adds the constraint again; see
[migrations](migrations.md#deferrable-constraints) for the declaration, the
migration it renders and the dialects that refuse it.

## Upgrading to 0.18.0

A `*vector.Vector` field tagged `read_only` now generates a
`momo.NullReadOnlyVectorColumn` instead of a `momo.ReadOnlyVectorColumn`, so
run `momo generate` and fix any helper that names the old type.

### A nullable read-only vector has its own column type

Before, `momo generate` gave a nullable read-only vector field the
non-nullable `momo.ReadOnlyVectorColumn[V]` and the field lost its null
handling, which `momo.NullReadOnlyColumn` gives a plain column. The generated
descriptor is now `momo.NullReadOnlyVectorColumn[V]`. The two types are not
convertible, so after you regenerate, a helper that takes the field as a
`momo.ReadOnlyVectorColumn[V]` no longer compiles. Make the helper take
`momo.VectorSource[V]`, which every vector column type satisfies, or take
`momo.NullReadOnlyVectorColumn[V]`. A non-pointer read-only vector field
keeps `momo.ReadOnlyVectorColumn[V]`. The read-only, create-only and immutable
vector types also stop converting into one another, as the scalar
permission columns already do.

## Upgrading to 0.17.0

`momo migrate drift` and the refusal of `momo migrate baseline` now name what
differs, and `drift --fix-sql` prints the repair; no edit is needed in your
code, but a script that reads the output of either on a database without momo
history sees a different report.

### Drift without history compares with the latest snapshot

On a database with no applied migration, `momo migrate drift` (and
`migrate.Engine.Drift`) used to report every table as `unmanaged`; it now compares the
live database with the latest snapshot in the migration directory, the schema
`baseline` expects, and reports `missing:`, `changed:` and `unmanaged:` objects
by name. A `changed:` line now ends with the live and snapshot definitions of
the fields that differ. The refusal of `migrate.Engine.Baseline` is a
`*migrate.BaselineMismatchError` that names the differing objects (the first 50)
and still matches `errors.Is(err, migrate.ErrBaselineMismatch)`.
`momo migrate drift --fix-sql` prints the DDL that brings the database to the
snapshot, withholding drops and column type changes unless `--allow-destructive`
is given; see [migrations](migrations.md#repairing-a-database-drift---fix-sql).

## Upgrading to 0.16.0

`momo.sum` has a new format 2 that an older momo binary refuses with
`migrate.ErrNewerFormat`, so upgrade every binary that reads a migration
directory (CI included) before `momo migrate hash` rewrites it; apart from that,
no edit is needed in your code.

### `momo.sum` format 2 and parallel migration branches

Format 2 is one checksum line per file with no directory hash. It is written
by `momo migrate hash`, while `diff` and `new --custom` leave a format 1 file as
it is; run `momo migrate hash --sum-format 1` to keep format 1. Two branches
that each add a migration for different tables now merge with `git merge`, plus
`momo migrate hash` when `.gitattributes` has no `momo.sum merge=union` rule,
and validate; a fork of the same table stays a `migrate.ErrBranchConflict` that
names the table, and `momo migrate rebase --renumber` moves pending migrations
after the newest applied one. See [migrations](migrations.md#parallel-branches).

### Importers write composite indexes

The GORM, Bun and Ent importers now write a composite index of the source model
as a `c.Index` declaration in a `MomoConfig` method of the generated model, so a
converted project no longer drops it on its next migration; rerun the import to
get the declaration.

### Declare a value-list check

`Config.CheckIn` declares a check over a list of values that `migrate diff`
compares as a set; `momo generate --from-db` now writes a constraint of that
shape as a `Config.CheckIn` declaration, and a snapshot written without the
value list still diffs as before. On SQLite a named table-level
`CHECK (col IN (...))` now inspects as a check with a value list, and
`--from-db` writes it as `Config.CheckIn`, instead of as an enum column; an
unnamed column check is unchanged.

### Clone a template database in tests

`momotest.WithTemplateClone` makes `momotest.New` clone a template database per
test instead of building a schema per test; without the option `momotest.New`
behaves as before.

### Declare a standalone sequence

A PostgreSQL sequence that no column owns, such as the one a column default
names with `nextval('jobs_seq')`, is now part of the schema model:
`momo generate --from-db` writes a `c.Sequence` call for it and keeps it in the
init snapshot, and `momo migrate` creates, alters, drops and compares it like
any other object, so an init migration built from such a database applies on an
empty one. Declare one with `momo.Config.Sequence` in a model's `MomoConfig`, for example
`c.Sequence("jobs_seq").Start(1000).Increment(10)`; the chain of
`momo.SequenceOpts` sets the schema, the data type, the bounds, the cache and
`Cycle`. Run `momo generate --from-db` again to adopt the sequences of an
existing database: a database that already uses one shows it as an
`unmanaged: sequence` line in `momo migrate drift` until the models declare it,
and `migrate.exclude` hides one you do not want managed. The snapshot gets an
optional `sequences` key and its `format_version` does not change, so snapshots
written before it still load. A release that predates the key reads a snapshot
that has it and ignores the sequences without an error, so move every machine
that writes snapshots to this release together. Declaring a sequence while
generating for SQLite, MySQL or MariaDB is refused, because those dialects have
no sequence in the schema model.

### Change a primary key with `AllowKeyChange`

`UpdateQuery.AllowKeyChange` is an opt-in that lets `UpdateQuery.Set` assign a
primary-key column, for a row whose key a user chooses and may rename. Without
it an assignment to a key column is refused with `ErrValidation`, as before.
With it the statement runs as written, on every dialect, and a key that
collides with another row fails with `ErrUniqueViolation`; foreign keys
declared `ON UPDATE CASCADE` follow the new key. `UpdateQuery.Model`,
`BulkUpdate`, the `OnUpdate` field hook and an identity key keep refusing a key
assignment.

## Upgrading to 0.15.0

No edit is needed in your code. A model can now declare full-text search, and
the declaration is recorded in the model and in the schema snapshot. On
PostgreSQL 12 or newer `momo migrate` renders it as a stored generated tsvector
column with a GIN index. On SQLite it renders an external-content FTS5 table
with sync triggers. On MySQL
and MariaDB a migration renders it as a `FULLTEXT` index, with `WITH PARSER`
when a parser is declared. A unique index, a column that is not text, more than
16 columns and a parser name other than `ngram` or `mecab` are refused with
`ErrValidation`; `AutoMigrate` also refuses a declaration on a table the
database holds with a storage engine other than InnoDB. A parser on MariaDB is
refused with `ErrUnsupported` when the engine knows the server is MariaDB (any
engine built on a driver); the offline `momo migrate` commands, which open no
database, cannot know it and render the parser, so MariaDB rejects it when the
migration is applied. Drift does not report a table for its storage engine.
Package `fts` also gains a query layer that reads the declaration: `fts.Over`
names the searched columns, and `fts.Search`, `fts.Score` and `fts.Snippet`
render a match, a relevance score and an excerpt, with the text of a `fts.Web`,
`fts.Plain` or `fts.Raw` query bound as a parameter. On PostgreSQL they search
the generated tsvector column `<index>_tsv` of the declaration; on SQLite they
search the FTS5 table `<table>_fts`, and a search whose FTS5 table does not
exist fails with `momo.ErrUnsupported` naming the table. The existing `fts`
builders keep their signatures and their PostgreSQL SQL. On the cgo SQLite
driver FTS5 needs the build flag `-tags sqlite_fts5` (or
`CGO_CFLAGS=-DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS5`); the pure-Go driver `driver/sqlitepure`
includes FTS5. On MySQL and MariaDB the same functions render
`MATCH(...) AGAINST (? IN BOOLEAN MODE)` over the `FULLTEXT` index of the
declaration, with a boolean-mode string built from the parsed words only, so
no typed character acts as an operator; the columns given to `fts.Over` must be
exactly the indexed columns in their order, and `fts.Snippet` fails with
`momo.ErrUnsupported`. `fts.MySQLMatch` and `fts.MySQLRelevance` take a mode
and a text of your own. A `MATCH` without a `FULLTEXT` index over exactly its
columns is `momo.ErrValidation`. InnoDB does not index a word shorter than
`innodb_ft_min_token_size` (3 by default), and a stopword of its list (such as
`the` or `it`) in a required term matches nothing, so a search that needs such a
word finds nothing; a row inserted in an open transaction is not found by a search until the
transaction commits. `momo.HybridSearch` now also runs on SQLite (FTS5 and
sqlite-vec) and MariaDB 11.8: `HybridSpec.Text` must be a column of the model's
full-text declaration, `TextConfig` is ignored there, and the query text is read
like an `fts.Web` query; MySQL has no vector distance function and fails the
build with `momo.ErrUnsupported`. PostgreSQL SQL and arguments are unchanged.

### Declare full-text search on a model

A model can declare one full-text search index, either with the `search` tag on
each text field (the index is named `<table>_search` and covers the tagged
fields in field order) or with `c.FullText(name, &m.A, &m.B)` in `MomoConfig`,
chained with `Config`, `Weights`, `Tokenizer`, `Parser` or `Expression` for the
options a dialect honours. `momo generate` rejects the tag on a column that is
not text, a second declaration on one table, and a configuration, tokenizer or
parser name outside a strict allowlist. Snapshots written before the
declaration load unchanged.

On PostgreSQL the declaration needs a `Config` (the text search configuration,
for example `english`), is pinned in the generation expression, and any change
of the declaration (`Columns`, `Config`, `Weights` or `Expression`) drops the
index, recreates the generated column and creates the index again. The
generated column is named `<index>_tsv`; a model column of that name, a source
column the table does not have, an index name that makes the column name longer
than 63 bytes fails with `ErrValidation`. A full-text index declared with
`c.FullText(...).Concurrently()` is built with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in the trailing
`-- momo:no-transaction` migration; the generated column, and the drop of the
old index when the declaration changes, stay in the transactional migration
before it. That drop is a plain `DROP INDEX`, not `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY`: it
runs inside the transaction that recreates the generated column and holds an
`ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on the table for that step.

On SQLite the declaration becomes an external-content FTS5 table named
`<table>_fts` plus three triggers (`<table>_fts_ai`, `_ad` and `_au`) that keep
it in step with the table, and the table is filled with the FTS5 `rebuild`
command when it is created. The table needs a rowid table with a primary key of
one `INTEGER` column; any other key, or a declared column the table lacks, is
`ErrValidation` naming the table. Removing the declaration, or the table, drops
the triggers, then the FTS5 table. Renaming the table drops and re-creates the
FTS5 table and the triggers under the new name. A build without FTS5 fails the
migration with `ErrUnsupported`. `INSERT OR REPLACE` and `ON CONFLICT REPLACE`
do not fire the delete trigger unless `PRAGMA recursive_triggers = ON`, which
leaves stale tokens in the FTS5 table; repair it with
`INSERT INTO <table>_fts(<table>_fts) VALUES('rebuild')`.

## Upgrading to 0.14.0

No edit is needed in your code. `Merge` and `BulkUpdate` now run on SQLite,
MySQL and MariaDB, where they returned `ErrUnsupported`, so code that relied on
the error (a fallback branch, a test that expects the refusal) now takes the
success path. A long `BulkUpdate` list is also chunked instead of refused on
every dialect.

### `BulkUpdate` runs on every dialect

SQLite renders `UPDATE ... FROM`, like PostgreSQL. MySQL and MariaDB render
`UPDATE t JOIN (SELECT ... UNION ALL SELECT ...) AS v ON ... SET ...`.
`RowsAffected` counts the rows that match a listed key on every dialect,
whether or not a value changed (the MySQL driver sets `clientFoundRows`).
`Returning` stays `ErrUnsupported` on MySQL and MariaDB, which have no
`UPDATE ... RETURNING`.

### A long list is chunked, not refused

`BulkUpdate(...).Exec` used to fail with `ErrLimitExceeded` when the list bound
more parameters than the dialect allows. It now splits the list into
statements, run in order and summed, atomically: in one transaction on a `DB`,
in a savepoint on a `Tx`. A `DB` pinned with `OnConn` cannot begin a
transaction, so a chunked list there is `ErrUnsupported`; call it on a `Tx`.
`SQL()` and `Rows` still render one statement and return `ErrLimitExceeded` over
the limit. If you split lists by hand to stay under the limit, you can drop that
code; a list split by hand and run in separate transactions stays valid.

### `BulkUpdateKeys` for a composite key

`BulkUpdateKeys(q, keys, cols, rows)` takes several key columns; each row holds
the key values first, then one value per column. `BulkUpdate` is the
single-key form and is unchanged. A NULL key value matches no row. A key listed
twice applies one of its rows, and which one is not defined.

### `Merge` runs on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB

`Merge(...).Exec` on a dialect without `MERGE` runs the same clauses as a
sequence of statements in one transaction (a savepoint on a `Tx`). It copies the
source into a temporary table, computes once the pairs of target and source rows
that `On` joins, with the new value of every assigned column taken from the
target row as it was before the statement, and then updates and inserts from
those two tables. Without concurrent writers the final table and the
affected-row count (rows updated plus rows inserted) are those of PostgreSQL,
also when the update changes a column that `On` reads or an assignment reads
another assigned column. A `NULL` key matches nothing. A target row that two
source rows match fails with `ErrTooManyRows` before anything is written when
there is a `WhenMatchedUpdate` clause. PostgreSQL's cardinality violation
(SQLSTATE 21000) is now `ErrTooManyRows` as well, so `errors.Is` agrees across
dialects; before, it had no momo kind.

Things that differ from PostgreSQL, and are refused or reported instead of
guessed:

- Under concurrent writers the sequence is not the single statement: a target
  row committed between its steps that starts to match is not seen, so the
  insert writes it again (or fails on a unique key), and the affected-row count
  is taken before the update. MySQL and MariaDB lock and re-read the matched
  target rows; SQLite fails with a busy error instead of reading stale data.
  See [capabilities](capabilities.md#merge-on-sqlite-mysql-and-mariadb).
- `Returning` (and `Rows`) is `ErrUnsupported`: the rows would come from a
  snapshot, not from the statement. `SET col = DEFAULT` in the update is
  `ErrUnsupported` too.
- `WhenMatchedUpdate` on a model without a primary key is `ErrUnsupported`,
  because a target row matched twice could not be detected.
- A `Merge` on a pinned `DB` is `ErrUnsupported`: it needs a transaction.
- `MergeQuery.SQL` has no single text on these dialects and returns
  `ErrUnsupported`; `MergeQuery.Statements` lists the statements `Exec` runs.
- The server account needs the privilege to create temporary tables, and the
  source needs distinct column names (alias `a.id` and `b.id`). On MySQL and
  MariaDB the temporary tables take the types and collations the server derives
  for them, so read the source from a table rather than from literals when a
  text key is compared with a column of another collation; a canceled context
  can leave the tables on that connection until its next `Merge`. See
  [MySQL and MariaDB](mysql.md#emulated-features).

## Upgrading to 0.13.0

No edit is needed in your code. Several calls that returned `ErrUnsupported` on
some dialects now return results (`DistinctOn` on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB,
`DELETE ... USING` and mixed `DEFAULT` rows in a multi-row insert on SQLite,
`Delete(...).Returning(...)` on MariaDB, and the `advisory` session functions on
MySQL and MariaDB), so code that relied on the error (a fallback branch, a test
that expects the refusal) now takes the success path.

### `DELETE ... USING` runs on SQLite

`DeleteQuery.Using` on SQLite renders
`DELETE FROM t WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM src WHERE ...)`, because SQLite has
no `USING`. A target row is deleted once if at least one source row satisfies
`Where`, which is what `USING` means on PostgreSQL, and it works with a
composite primary key and a table without one. SQLite's `RETURNING` reads the
deleted table only, so `Returning` accepts columns of the target; a column of a
`Using` source is still `ErrUnsupported` there. A workaround that put a
subquery in `Where` keeps working. Two rules apply on every dialect. A `Using`
source with the target's own name is now `ErrValidation` (PostgreSQL already
refused it; on SQLite it would have bound every column to the inner table):
alias it with `TableRef.As` to join a table to itself. And qualify every column
in a raw `Where` fragment and in interceptor predicates: on SQLite an
unqualified column that the target and a source share binds to the source,
where PostgreSQL reports it as ambiguous.

### Mixed `DEFAULT` rows in a multi-row insert run on SQLite

`Models` with a `dbdefault` field that is zero in some rows and set in others,
and `ValuesRows` with a column that is omitted or `SetDefault` in some rows and
given in others, failed with `ErrUnsupported` on SQLite, which cannot put
`DEFAULT` in a `VALUES` list. `Exec` and `Rows` now split the rows into runs of
consecutive rows that leave the same columns to the database default and insert
each run as its own statement, in order, inside one transaction (a savepoint
inside a `Tx`). The stored defaults are read back into the models as before,
and `Rows` returns the rows in the order you gave. An insert that alternates
between patterns costs one statement per change. `SQL` renders one statement,
so it still fails with `ErrUnsupported` for such a mix, as do `Unnest` and
`Copy`; a `WITH` clause on a split insert is `ErrValidation`, and a split
insert on a connection pinned with `OnConn`, which cannot open the transaction,
fails with `ErrUnsupported` before any statement runs. Other dialects are
unchanged. PostgreSQL and MariaDB still write `DEFAULT` inline in one statement
for `Models`. MySQL has no `RETURNING`, so `Models` with a zero `dbdefault`
field still fails there with `ErrUnsupported`, as before. `ValuesRows` writes
`DEFAULT` inline on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB.

### `DistinctOn` on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB

`SelectQuery.DistinctOn` returned `ErrUnsupported` on SQLite, MySQL and
MariaDB. It now runs on all of them, emulated with a window function, and
keeps the first row of each group of the leading `OrderBy` keys, the
tie-breakers after them deciding which row is first, and all rows with a NULL
key forming one group, as PostgreSQL's `DISTINCT ON` does when the `OrderBy` is
total (see the NULLS point below). A derived table
numbers the rows of each group with `ROW_NUMBER()` and the outer query keeps
number 1. It needs SQLite 3.25, MySQL 8.0 or MariaDB 10.2, the versions that
have window functions. PostgreSQL is unchanged.

What to check:

- The `OrderBy` rule is the same on every dialect: the leading items must be the
  `DistinctOn` expressions, in any order, and an `OrderBy` is required
  (`ErrValidation` otherwise). A query that built on PostgreSQL builds on the
  others.
- The helper column never reaches your scan or a raw read of the statement. Each
  result column keeps the name of its column or its `As` alias; a bare function
  in the select list has no such name there, so alias it with `As`.
- An `OrderBy` on a column that is not in the select list works. An `OrderBy`
  on an `As` alias is allowed when the alias is in the select list.
- `Count` and `Exists` count the groups, as on PostgreSQL. `Where`, joins,
  `GroupBy`, `Having` and keyset `After` filter before the dedupe; `Limit` and
  `Offset` apply after it.
- A row lock (`ForUpdate`, `ForShare`) with `DistinctOn` is `ErrUnsupported` on
  these dialects, because the rows are read in a derived table and the lock
  would not cover the rows returned. PostgreSQL refuses the combination with
  `ErrValidation`.
- Servers place NULLs differently by default (PostgreSQL last in an ascending
  order and first in a descending one, the others the reverse). For an
  `OrderBy` item on a nullable model column or `NullColumn` with no NULLS term,
  momo writes PostgreSQL's placement out, so the same row wins on every
  dialect. It cannot know that a `ColumnOf` column or an expression is
  nullable: give those an explicit `NullsFirst` or `NullsLast`, or the tiebreak
  can pick a different row than PostgreSQL does.
- A subquery or CTE that reads an unaliased select-list expression by the name
  PostgreSQL gives it must alias it with `As`: on the emulated dialects that
  column is `momo_cN`. Columns and `As` aliases keep their names.
- `Count` and `Exists` count the groups without repeating the select list, so a
  join that selects two columns of the same name works on MySQL too.
- An `As` alias is checked as everywhere else: an empty, malformed or
  over-long alias is `ErrValidation` on every dialect.

### `DELETE ... RETURNING` on MariaDB

`Delete(...).Returning(...)`, `ReturningAll` and `DeleteQuery.One` on MariaDB
now run `DELETE ... RETURNING` (MariaDB 10.0.5 or later), through the new
`DeleteReturning` capability of the MariaDB dialect.

Three cases keep the refusal. MySQL has no `DELETE ... RETURNING`, so a delete
with `Returning` there is still `ErrUnsupported`, and the message names MariaDB
as the alternative. A `Delete` with `Using` is a multi-table `DELETE`, which
MariaDB refuses with `RETURNING`, so that combination is `ErrUnsupported` on
the MySQL family. `UPDATE ... RETURNING` does not exist on MariaDB and stays
`ErrUnsupported`. `INSERT ... RETURNING` on MariaDB is unchanged. See
[MySQL and MariaDB](mysql.md#capabilities).

### Advisory session locks on MySQL and MariaDB

The `advisory` session functions (`advisory.Lock`, `advisory.TryLock`,
`advisory.Unlock` and their text-key forms such as `advisory.LockString`) used
to return `ErrUnsupported` on MySQL and MariaDB. They now run `GET_LOCK`, `GET_LOCK(name, 0)` and `RELEASE_LOCK` on
a pinned connection (`db.OnConn(pc)`), as they do on PostgreSQL with
`pg_advisory_lock`. Take the pinned `*momo.DB` from `momo.Pinner`, lock and
unlock on it, and unlock before you release the connection to the pool; a pooled
`*momo.DB` is `ErrValidation`. What differs from PostgreSQL:

- The lock name is `momo:advisory:<db>:<key>` and is scoped to the current
  database, as a PostgreSQL advisory lock is (`GET_LOCK` names are otherwise
  global to the server): `<db>` is 8 hex digits of `sha256(DATABASE())`, or
  `nodb` without a default database. An `int64` key is `<key>` in decimal, and a
  text key is `s:` plus 32 hex digits of its sha256. `advisory.Hash64` has no
  effect, and a text key is a different lock than the one PostgreSQL takes for
  the same string.
- `advisory.Lock` waits in one-second `GET_LOCK` calls until the lock is granted
  or the context ends. After it returns an error, `Discard` the pinned
  connection instead of releasing it, because a granted lock may still be
  attached to it.
- The transaction-scoped functions (`advisory.XactLock` and the rest) and the
  shared functions (`advisory.LockShared` and the rest) stay `ErrUnsupported`: a
  `GET_LOCK` lock is not released by a commit or rollback and has no shared mode.

See [MySQL](mysql.md#advisory-locks) for the details.

## Upgrading to 0.12.0

Two changes can need an edit. `momo.Avg` is now generic, so code that uses it
as an uninstantiated function value must write `momo.Avg[float64]` (see
"Aggregates over integer and `types.Numeric` columns" below). And
`momo generate --from-db --schema` is now a usage error on MySQL and MariaDB,
which ignored the flag before, so a script that passes it there must drop it (see "`momo generate --from-db` reads SQLite" below). Otherwise no
change is needed in your code. Three things can change what a command does,
all below: a `momo.yaml` that lists several dialects, a MySQL or MariaDB
schema that the library generated earlier, and a SQLite `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`
that inspection now reports as NOT NULL, which can show one rebuild in the
next `momo migrate diff`. Several calls that returned
`ErrUnsupported` on some dialects now return results, so code that relied on
the error (a fallback branch, a test that expects the refusal) now takes the
success path. Check the semantic differences below before you drop a
workaround.

### `momo migrate` runs on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB

Before this release `momo migrate` ran the PostgreSQL dialect alone and exited 2
for any other. It now runs every subcommand on SQLite (`--dialect sqlite`) and on MySQL and
MariaDB (`--dialect mysql`; one dialect for both servers). A project with a
single PostgreSQL dialect behaves as before. One thing does change: with
`dialects: [sqlite, postgres]` in `momo.yaml`, `--dialect postgres` used to read
the models for the first listed dialect (SQLite) and now reads them for the one
you chose, so `diff` writes PostgreSQL column types. If you worked around the old
behaviour by reordering `dialects`, you no longer need to; check the next
`diff` of such a project. For the new dialects:

- SQLite uses the pure-Go driver, so the `momo` binary still needs no cgo. The
  URL is a file path, a `file:` URI or `sqlite:///path.db`.
- MySQL and MariaDB take a `mysql://` or `mariadb://` URL, or a go-sql-driver
  DSN, and the URL must name a database.
- `momo generate` and `momo migrate diff` now map Go types to MySQL and
  MariaDB column types (`gen/typemap`); before, every field failed with
  `ErrUnsupported` there.
- DDL is not transactional on MySQL and MariaDB: a failed `apply` leaves the
  statements that ran, and `status` shows the migration as `dirty` until
  `resolve` settles it.
- On MySQL and MariaDB a string without `size:N` is `text`, which the servers
  cannot use in a primary key, unique key or index (error 1170). The generator
  refuses such a schema, naming the column and asking for `size:N`, before
  anything is written. The same holds for a blob or json column in a key.
- A `types.Numeric` with a `precision` tag is `decimal(p,s)` on MySQL and
  MariaDB; before, the library generated `text` for it. A schema that an earlier
  release generated for these servers gets an `ALTER ... text` to
  `decimal(p,s)` on the next `diff`, which rewrites the column and fails on a
  value that is not a number. `decimal` cannot hold `NaN` or an infinity,
  so a `types.Numeric` that carries one is refused when it is written. A precision without a scale means scale 0. The generator checks
  that the precision is at most 65, the scale at most 30 and the scale not
  above the precision. Without a `precision` tag the column stays `text`.

### `ILike` on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB

`momo.ILike` no longer fails on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB. They render
`LOWER(x) LIKE LOWER(?) ESCAPE '!'`; `momo.Not(momo.ILike(...))` is NOT ILIKE.
PostgreSQL is unchanged. The results are not identical to PostgreSQL:

- SQLite folds ASCII letters only, so `Ä` does not match `ä`. PostgreSQL folds
  it. This is the reason the call was refused before.
- MySQL and MariaDB fold with `LOWER`, but the comparison follows the column
  collation. Momo does not add a `_ci` or `_ai` collation: the default
  `_ai_ci` collations are accent-insensitive (`a` matches `ä`), which
  PostgreSQL `ILIKE` is not.
- An index on the column is not used, because the column is inside `LOWER`.
- On MySQL and MariaDB the column must be a character type. On `BINARY`,
  `VARBINARY` and `BLOB` columns `LOWER` does nothing and `LIKE` is
  case-sensitive, so the match is case-sensitive there. Momo adds no `CONVERT`.

The capability flags `dialect.Dialect.ILike` and `dialect.Dialect.NullsOrdering`
keep meaning native syntax: they stay false on MySQL (and `ILike` on SQLite)
while the features work.

### `NullsFirst` and `NullsLast` on MySQL and MariaDB

An explicit NULLS placement, on a column, an `Order` from `momo.Asc` or
`momo.Desc`, or `momo.OrderByPredicate`, renders `(e IS NULL) DESC, e ASC` or
`(e IS NULL) ASC, e ASC` (with the direction of the item), which orders exactly
as PostgreSQL. The expression is rendered twice, so a value it binds appears
twice among the arguments, in order. `After` over a nullable key was and is
`ErrUnsupported`. The outer `OrderBy` of a `SelectUnion` with a NULLS term is
`ErrUnsupported` on MySQL and MariaDB, and so is a window with a `Range` frame
that has an offset and one `OrderBy` item with a NULLS term: the emulation adds
a second sort key and the server needs exactly one (error 3587). Drop the NULLS
term or use a `Rows` frame. If you wrote `OrderByPredicate` as a
workaround, it still works and you can switch to `NullsLast`.

### Aggregate `Filter` on MySQL and MariaDB

`momo.Agg.Filter` and `agg.Call.Filter` render `agg(CASE WHEN p THEN x END)`,
and `COUNT(*)` becomes `COUNT(CASE WHEN p THEN 1 END)`. This is exact for the
aggregates that skip NULLs: `Sum`, `Avg`, `Min`, `Max`, `CountOf`,
`CountDistinct`, `agg.String`, and `agg.Func` over `count`, `sum`, `avg`,
`min`, `max` and the `std` and `var` family, also with `Over`. A call that
keeps NULLs (`agg.JSONB`, any other `agg.Func`) is still `ErrUnsupported` there,
with a message that says why; so is `agg.Func` over a raw `*` (use
`momo.CountAll().Filter(p)`). `Builder.AppendFilter` itself still fails on
MySQL: a custom aggregate rewrites its own arguments.

### `generate --from-db --check` compares the body, not only the header hash

No change is needed. A model file written by `momo generate --from-db` that
you edited by hand used to be reported as stale (`--check`) or as a conflict
with a `.new` file (plain run) whenever the database now held your edit too,
because the `// momo:fromdb sha256=...` header still carried the hash of the
old body. Now a file whose body equals the regenerated body is current: `--check`
passes, and a plain run rewrites only the header line. A file whose body
differs is still stale or a conflict, and `momo generate` without `--from-db`
is unchanged.

### `sqlfn.Greatest`, `sqlfn.Least`, `sqlfn.Floor`, `sqlfn.Ceil` and `jsonop.TypeOf`

No change is needed; these are new functions. They replace the raw SQL or the
untyped `momo.Func` calls that a per-row setting read from JSON needed
(`GREATEST(1, CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(v) = 'number' THEN floor(...) ELSE ... END)`):

```text
years := sqlfn.Greatest[float64](momo.Lit(1.0),
    sqlfn.Case[float64]().WhenExpr(jsonop.TypeOf(v).Eq("number"), floored).Else(fallback))
```

- `sqlfn.Greatest` and `sqlfn.Least` ignore NULL arguments and are NULL only when
  every argument is NULL, on every dialect. That is PostgreSQL's rule; MySQL,
  MariaDB and SQLite return NULL for any NULL argument, so Momo rewrites each
  argument `x` to `COALESCE(x, the other arguments)` there. The rewrite renders
  every argument once per argument, so keep the list short. `types.Numeric` is
  PostgreSQL only and fails with `momo.ErrUnsupported` elsewhere, as the
  `sqlfn` arithmetic does.
- `sqlfn.Floor` and `sqlfn.Ceil` take a float or a `types.Numeric` and return
  the same type (an integer needs a `sqlfn.Cast` first, because PostgreSQL's
  `floor` of an integer is `double precision`). SQLite is rendered with
  `CAST` rather than `floor()`, which the mattn driver lacks without its
  `sqlite_math_functions` build tag. `types.Numeric` is PostgreSQL only.
- `jsonop.TypeOf` is `jsonb_typeof`. SQLite's `json_type` and MySQL and
  MariaDB's `JSON_TYPE` are mapped to the same six names: `object`, `array`,
  `string`, `number`, `boolean` and `null`. A SQL NULL column gives SQL NULL.

### MySQL and MariaDB: graph writes, `FindOrCreate` and upsert targets

Calls that returned `ErrUnsupported` on MySQL or MariaDB now work. No existing
working code changes behaviour.

- `momo.CreateGraph` works on MySQL and MariaDB. MariaDB reads the generated
  keys with `INSERT ... RETURNING`. MySQL reads `LAST_INSERT_ID` after each
  statement and inserts has-many and many-to-many children one row per
  statement inside the graph's transaction, so every key is exact whatever
  `innodb_autoinc_lock_mode` is. A bulk of children that mixes zero and explicit
  keys is `ErrValidation` on MySQL.
- `momo.FindOrCreate` works on MySQL and MariaDB. It runs in a transaction as a
  plain insert and, on a unique violation, re-selects the row by key with a
  shared-lock read, so a call that finds an existing row costs one failed
  insert and one select.
- An upsert on a unique key other than the primary key is accepted on MySQL and
  MariaDB when every other unique key is made only of auto-increment columns
  the insert leaves out: an auto-increment primary key next to `UNIQUE(email)`,
  upserting on `email` with a zero identity. Every other case is still
  `ErrUnsupported`, and the error now says which unique key is the problem.
- A plain multi-row `Models` insert on MySQL still writes no keys back.

### `momo generate --from-db` reads MySQL and MariaDB

Besides PostgreSQL, the command now inspects a MySQL 8.4, MySQL 9.7 or
MariaDB 11.8 database when `momo.yaml` sets `dialects: [mysql]`. A project that
sets `dialects: [postgres]` or sets none behaves as before. See
[MySQL and MariaDB](mysql.md#models-from-a-database).

### A comma inside parentheses in a tag option

The tag parser now keeps a comma that sits inside balanced parentheses in one
option, so `type:decimal(10,2)` is read as one option, and inside parentheses it
skips a single-quoted value, so `type:enum('a)b','c')` is one option too.
